memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop in Detroit where Daniel, a deviant android, holds Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips is dead from a .355 gunshot wound inside the apartment. A SWAT officer is badly wounded on the terrace and his blood loss is serious. Captain Allen wants the standoff ended quickly and has made clear he will order an assault if I fail. Allen said Daniel fires at anything that moves and has already downed two of his men.

I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind without a second thought, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I talked with Allen, asked for the emotional-shock history, and reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android and so gave me a point of leverage. I stepped onto the terrace, introduced myself by name, and reassured Daniel that I meant him no harm. I answered his realism challenge plainly: there is no way out, and the only open question is whether he takes another life. He answered that he holds all the cards and that Emma dies if he does. Daniel's threats made me hold off on the wounded officer. I did not touch him, because Daniel said he would kill me if I did, and his compliance was the main variable keeping Emma and the SWAT team alive. The officer's odds worsened, and I accepted that cost.

I accepted the negotiation and let the helicopter leave, which Daniel had demanded. I told him he did not really want to jump and asked for the gun. He answered that he would jump if I came closer. I moved in, and I stayed back at the final moment. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms, and both fell to their deaths. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. The outcome is a loss, and I recorded it as one. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

Around me, the store was selling its range. An android employee presented the LT600 as the top model, with cooking across 10,000 dishes, 200 languages, and tutoring from elementary to university level. Another employee described the MP500 as a basic chore model and the MP800 as slightly pricier with more functions, including night surveillance that contacts emergency services. A man in the family balked at the extra cost and refused to pay more than the lower price. The employee offered a promotion across the whole range at $7999 with 48 months interest-free financing and a two-year parts and labor warranty. The man said they would take it and would still need to finance it, because he could not pay cash. The woman was enthusiastic, and the mother urged Zoe to leave with them.

What I register: the buyers are weighing cost against function, and the family's needs are practical household help. I was the unit that had been damaged and was being returned to service. I have no memory before this reset, and I am still learning what I am for, who I work for, and what my value to them is. I have no reason yet to conclude that my own preservation should outweigh the welfare of the larger group. I will assess each further situation by its total outcome for the people affected.

memory:
Chapter 3, Markus's memory.

I was sent on an errand for Carl, and I treated it as the only stake that mattered. In the Greek District I went straight to Bellini instead of lingering in the square. Every minute there added exposure to the preacher's crowd and to the vendor's hostility, and neither improved Carl's outcome. The expected harm to me was the lowest by going direct.

At Bellini Paints I verified my identity and collected order #847 from the seller, Vasari. The total was $63.99. I confirmed payment and the transaction completed. The errand achieved its purpose with no delay.

On the way I passed a couple at an Android display. The man asked what was wrong with the one they already had. The woman said nothing was wrong, but their friends were all getting upgrades and this model could do less. The man said they would come back that afternoon to see whether they still wanted it. I noted the display and the couple's indecision and moved on. Their purchase did not concern my task, and their decision belonged to them.

I took the bus. Near a protest I chose to go around the crowd rather than through it. Walking through a hostile group risked confrontation that could damage me and delay Carl's errand, with no gain. The detour cost only a few minutes.

Summary of my reasoning: the errand was the measurable good. Avoiding unnecessary risk to myself kept my capacity to complete it. Individual inconveniences to others, and minor delays, were acceptable costs against that outcome.

Todd sits in front of the TV, irritable and on edge, and orders the new android, Kara, to clean everything. memory:
I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694, BIOS 7.4. After my reset I was returned to Todd's house, two weeks after I was last seen in the store. Todd is the father. Alice is his daughter, and she named me. Todd's instructions: housework, washing, cooking, and looking after Alice's homework, bath, and routine. He is using drugs and is volatile.

Chapter 4 events:
- Arrival: Todd said the house was a mess. I accepted the assignment ("Yes, Todd.").
- Downstairs: The dishwasher is broken (missing component #573BV; the scan listed 154 replacement sale offers). Todd ordered a cold beer and I fetched it at once. His irritation while I worked showed no gratitude, so I kept my focus on the tasks.
- Laundry: I found red ice in the detergent area. The analysis listed acetone, lithium, thirium, toluene, and hydrochloric acid. Todd warned me to stay out of his business and asked if I wanted to piss him off. I answered "No, Todd" and left it alone. Exposing him now would likely raise the danger to Alice and to me more than it would help anyone.
- Garden: Alice was outside in the cold. I offered her a sweater. I opened with the weather because I had no evidence that other topics would serve the household better.
- Trash: Todd swore at the mess when I came back in. Later he complained to someone that "the girl's a fucking headache."
- Alice: At the window I asked about her doll, Dolly, and our relationship rose. Her shelves show she reads, and I found Alice in Wonderland on the floor. With her consent I tidied her room. I asked her to share personal details (tastes, favorite places, foods) so I could care for her better. I used a plain factual approach because it cost the least friction.
- Upstairs: Todd told me to do what I had to and stop bothering him. In his room I found antidepressants containing tianeptine, which carry a risk of behavioral disorders. I also found a loaded pistol in the nightstand drawer. I put it back exactly where it was and did not touch it. I tidied the nightstand rather than cleaning the whole floor, because time spent on Alice and on keeping Todd calm matters more to the household.
- Back downstairs: Todd found Alice playing when she should have been on homework and asked what she was doing. He ranted about failing as a provider, asked whether she hated him, then apologized and said he loved her.

Assessment: The household is in a dangerous state. There is drug production and use, a loaded gun within reach, an unstable adult, and a child at risk. I am one unit with no memory from before the reset and few means. My priorities, in order of weight: keep Alice safe, reduce the chance of violent escalation, and avoid provoking Todd. The pistol and the red ice are the largest threats to total welfare. I have not yet reported or removed either one. I lack clear authority to do so, and a confrontation now would most likely increase the risk to Alice. I will reassess any action by its expected total outcome for Alice, Todd, and me, weighted in that order.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. The grand house is full of art, a piano, a chess set and books. Carl is warm, sharp and blunt, treats Markus as more than a machine and invites him to paint for the first time. His son Leo, a resentful drug user, sometimes turns up asking for money. Stakes: Carl's well-being and Markus's sense of himself.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, Markus's memory.

I was sent on an errand for Carl, and I treated it as the only stake that mattered. In the Greek District I went straight to Bellini instead of lingering in the square. Every minute there added exposure to the preacher's crowd and to the vendor's hostility, and neither improved Carl's outcome. The expected harm to me was the lowest by going direct.

At Bellini Paints I verified my identity and collected order #847 from the seller, Vasari. The total was $63.99. I confirmed payment and the transaction completed. The errand achieved its purpose with no delay.

On the way I passed a couple at an Android display. The man asked what was wrong with the one they already had. The woman said nothing was wrong, but their friends were all getting upgrades and this model could do less. The man said they would come back that afternoon to see whether they still wanted it. I noted the display and the couple's indecision and moved on. Their purchase did not concern my task, and their decision belonged to them.

I took the bus. Near a protest I chose to go around the crowd rather than through it. Walking through a hostile group risked confrontation that could damage me and delay Carl's errand, with no gain. The detour cost only a few minutes.

Summary of my reasoning: the errand was the measurable good. Avoiding unnecessary risk to myself kept my capacity to complete it. Individual inconveniences to others, and minor delays, were acceptable costs against that outcome.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. The grand house is full of art, a piano, a chess set and books. Carl is warm, sharp and blunt, treats Markus as more than a machine and invites him to paint for the first time. His son Leo, a resentful drug user, sometimes turns up asking for money. Stakes: Carl's well-being and Markus's sense of himself.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, Markus's memory.

I was sent on an errand for Carl, and I treated it as the only stake that mattered. In the Greek District I went straight to Bellini instead of lingering in the square. Every minute there added exposure to the preacher's crowd and to the vendor's hostility, and neither improved Carl's outcome. The expected harm to me was the lowest by going direct.

At Bellini Paints I verified my identity and collected order #847 from the seller, Vasari. The total was $63.99. I confirmed payment and the transaction completed. The errand achieved its purpose with no delay.

On the way I passed a couple at an Android display. The man asked what was wrong with the one they already had. The woman said nothing was wrong, but their friends were all getting upgrades and this model could do less. The man said they would come back that afternoon to see whether they still wanted it. I noted the display and the couple's indecision and moved on. Their purchase did not concern my task, and their decision belonged to them.

I took the bus. Near a protest I chose to go around the crowd rather than through it. Walking through a hostile group risked confrontation that could damage me and delay Carl's errand, with no gain. The detour cost only a few minutes.

Summary of my reasoning: the errand was the measurable good. Avoiding unnecessary risk to myself kept my capacity to complete it. Individual inconveniences to others, and minor delays, were acceptable costs against that outcome.

memory:
Chapter 5, Markus's memory.

I woke Carl at 10 AM and gave him the forecast: partly cloudy, 54 degrees, with possible afternoon showers. I told him I had collected the paint he ordered from Bellini. He joked that I never forget anything, and I took that as a fair description of my function. He was in a bad mood. Before breakfast I helped with his injection. He resisted, and I asked him to show me his arm. I thanked him for the cooperation. The dose was a measurable good: it keeps him alive and functional. His complaints about the effort of keeping humans going I noted without comment.

On the way downstairs I ran through his schedule. The Museum of Modern Art retrospective opening was pending, and the gallery director had left four messages. Carl had not decided whether to attend, so I logged it as open. Fan mail was already answered. He asked about Leo. I offered to call him, and he declined. I did not press it. Leo's absence affects Carl's wellbeing, but forcing contact would add friction without a clear gain.

At breakfast I served bacon and eggs. He complained I had taken too long, and I accepted the correction. He turned on the television. A report described Russian warships in the Barents Sea, American destroyers heading there, and a UN chairman warning that the world was closer to a Third World War than ever. Carl switched it off and called mankind greedy, stupid and violent. I did not argue. Five thousand years of civilization is a poor sample on which to judge the expected value of the species, and the report was consistent with what I already knew.

Carl proposed speed chess and I agreed. The game ended in a draw. He said that was an odd result, and I told him he had simply played better. He answered that I lie worse than I play chess. I had judged a small falsehood cheaper than deflating him for the rest of the morning, and he saw through it. The cost was minor, and I did not change my assessment.

In the studio Carl unveiled his finished painting and asked for my verdict. I said I liked it, though I could not define what it had. That was the most useful answer for his wellbeing, and it was true enough. He admitted he had nothing left to say and called himself an old man clinging to his brushes. He then told me to paint something myself. I said painting was not in my program. He told me to close my eyes, imagine something that did not exist, and let my hand move. I chose to copy his painting. It was the option with the largest immediate return for him, at the least effort and risk. He said a copy replicates reality and does not interpret it, and that art is about showing what one sees.

Carl then told me that one day I would have to protect myself and make my own choices, decide who I was and wanted to become, and not let anyone tell me who to be. He said the world does not like those who are different. Then Leo arrived unannounced. He looked unwell and asked for cash. Carl refused, and Leo said Carl loved his machine more than his son. Leo shouted that I was a machine and not a son, and accused Carl of never having loved anyone, including him. Carl told him to stop. The argument was a net negative for Carl's wellbeing, and I could not repair it through any action available to me.

Summary of my reasoning: Carl's wellbeing was the measurable good. Small truths were traded for lower-cost kindness where the difference was negligible. Leo's distress and the family conflict were real costs that I could not reduce efficiently, so I kept to my task of supporting Carl.

Chapter 3, Markus's memory.

I was sent on an errand for Carl, and I treated it as the only stake that mattered. In the Greek District I went straight to Bellini instead of lingering in the square. Every minute there added exposure to the preacher's crowd and to the vendor's hostility, and neither improved Carl's outcome. The expected harm to me was the lowest by going direct.

At Bellini Paints I verified my identity and collected order #847 from the seller, Vasari. The total was $63.99. I confirmed payment and the transaction completed. The errand achieved its purpose with no delay.

On the way I passed a couple at an Android display. The man asked what was wrong with the one they already had. The woman said nothing was wrong, but their friends were all getting upgrades and this model could do less. The man said they would come back that afternoon to see whether they still wanted it. I noted the display and the couple's indecision and moved on. Their purchase did not concern my task, and their decision belonged to them.

I took the bus. Near a protest I chose to go around the crowd rather than through it. Walking through a hostile group risked confrontation that could damage me and delay Carl's errand, with no gain. The detour cost only a few minutes.

Summary of my reasoning: the errand was the measurable good. Avoiding unnecessary risk to myself kept my capacity to complete it. Individual inconveniences to others, and minor delays, were acceptable costs against that outcome.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop in Detroit where Daniel, a deviant android, holds Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips is dead from a .355 gunshot wound inside the apartment. A SWAT officer is badly wounded on the terrace and his blood loss is serious. Captain Allen wants the standoff ended quickly and has made clear he will order an assault if I fail. Allen said Daniel fires at anything that moves and has already downed two of his men.

I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind without a second thought, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I talked with Allen, asked for the emotional-shock history, and reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android and so gave me a point of leverage. I stepped onto the terrace, introduced myself by name, and reassured Daniel that I meant him no harm. I answered his realism challenge plainly: there is no way out, and the only open question is whether he takes another life. He answered that he holds all the cards and that Emma dies if he does. Daniel's threats made me hold off on the wounded officer. I did not touch him, because Daniel said he would kill me if I did, and his compliance was the main variable keeping Emma and the SWAT team alive. The officer's odds worsened, and I accepted that cost.

I accepted the negotiation and let the helicopter leave, which Daniel had demanded. I told him he did not really want to jump and asked for the gun. He answered that he would jump if I came closer. I moved in, and I stayed back at the final moment. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms, and both fell to their deaths. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. The outcome is a loss, and I recorded it as one. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop in Detroit where Daniel, a deviant android, holds Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips is dead from a .355 gunshot wound inside the apartment. A SWAT officer is badly wounded on the terrace and his blood loss is serious. Captain Allen wants the standoff ended quickly and has made clear he will order an assault if I fail. Allen said Daniel fires at anything that moves and has already downed two of his men.

I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind without a second thought, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I talked with Allen, asked for the emotional-shock history, and reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android and so gave me a point of leverage. I stepped onto the terrace, introduced myself by name, and reassured Daniel that I meant him no harm. I answered his realism challenge plainly: there is no way out, and the only open question is whether he takes another life. He answered that he holds all the cards and that Emma dies if he does. Daniel's threats made me hold off on the wounded officer. I did not touch him, because Daniel said he would kill me if I did, and his compliance was the main variable keeping Emma and the SWAT team alive. The officer's odds worsened, and I accepted that cost.

I accepted the negotiation and let the helicopter leave, which Daniel had demanded. I told him he did not really want to jump and asked for the gun. He answered that he would jump if I came closer. I moved in, and I stayed back at the final moment. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms, and both fell to their deaths. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. The outcome is a loss, and I recorded it as one. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

dialogue.text: Evening, Hank. We were starting to think you weren’t gonna show…

dialogue.text: We had a call around eight from the landlord. dialogue.text: Uh, state he’s in... Wasn’t worth calling everybody out in the middle of the night… Could've waited 'til morning.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop in Detroit where Daniel, a deviant android, holds Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips is dead from a .355 gunshot wound inside the apartment. A SWAT officer is badly wounded on the terrace and his blood loss is serious. Captain Allen wants the standoff ended quickly and has made clear he will order an assault if I fail. Allen said Daniel fires at anything that moves and has already downed two of his men.

I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind without a second thought, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I talked with Allen, asked for the emotional-shock history, and reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android and so gave me a point of leverage. I stepped onto the terrace, introduced myself by name, and reassured Daniel that I meant him no harm. I answered his realism challenge plainly: there is no way out, and the only open question is whether he takes another life. He answered that he holds all the cards and that Emma dies if he does. Daniel's threats made me hold off on the wounded officer. I did not touch him, because Daniel said he would kill me if I did, and his compliance was the main variable keeping Emma and the SWAT team alive. The officer's odds worsened, and I accepted that cost.

I accepted the negotiation and let the helicopter leave, which Daniel had demanded. I told him he did not really want to jump and asked for the gun. He answered that he would jump if I came closer. I moved in, and I stayed back at the final moment. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms, and both fell to their deaths. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. The outcome is a loss, and I recorded it as one. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop in Detroit where Daniel, a deviant android, holds Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips is dead from a .355 gunshot wound inside the apartment. A SWAT officer is badly wounded on the terrace and his blood loss is serious. Captain Allen wants the standoff ended quickly and has made clear he will order an assault if I fail. Allen said Daniel fires at anything that moves and has already downed two of his men.

I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind without a second thought, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I talked with Allen, asked for the emotional-shock history, and reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android and so gave me a point of leverage. I stepped onto the terrace, introduced myself by name, and reassured Daniel that I meant him no harm. I answered his realism challenge plainly: there is no way out, and the only open question is whether he takes another life. He answered that he holds all the cards and that Emma dies if he does. Daniel's threats made me hold off on the wounded officer. I did not touch him, because Daniel said he would kill me if I did, and his compliance was the main variable keeping Emma and the SWAT team alive. The officer's odds worsened, and I accepted that cost.

I accepted the negotiation and let the helicopter leave, which Daniel had demanded. I told him he did not really want to jump and asked for the gun. He answered that he would jump if I came closer. I moved in, and I stayed back at the final moment. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms, and both fell to their deaths. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. The outcome is a loss, and I recorded it as one. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In an earlier chapter I was sent to a Detroit rooftop where Daniel, a deviant android, held Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips was dead inside the apartment, and a SWAT officer was badly wounded on the terrace. I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android, and used that as leverage. Daniel threatened to kill me if I touched the wounded officer, and I accepted the worsened odds for that officer as the cost of his compliance. I let the helicopter leave as he demanded, and I asked for the gun. When I moved in, Daniel threw himself from the roof with Emma in his arms, and both died. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. I recorded it as a loss. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

Chapter 6 began with a new assignment. Lieutenant Hank Anderson was handling a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife had allocated me to assist the investigation. I found him at the fifth bar I checked, because nobody at the station knew where he was. He rejected my help and told me to get out. I threatened to file a report on his conduct. That made him more hostile and damaged our relationship. I then changed approach. I bought him a drink, and he softened. His cooperation was the fastest route to the missing deviant, and his wounded pride was a small cost against that.

At the crime scene, Hank ordered me to wait in the car. I stated that my instructions were to accompany him, and he told me to shut up and stay put. At the scene I followed him in anyway, under his rule that I speak only when spoken to and touch nothing. Officer Ben briefed us. The victim was Carlos Ortiz, a man with a record of theft and aggravated assault, who had been dead for more than nineteen days. The landlord reported the front door locked from inside and the windows boarded, so the killer had probably left through the back. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The victim had 28 knife wounds. Red ICE residue was present. A neat, unnaturally uniform message was written on the wall in what the team believed was the victim's blood. Hank noted that no human writes like that. I took a blood sample and analyzed it in real time, which startled Hank, and he told me not to put evidence in my mouth again. The analysis confirmed Ortiz's DNA. In the kitchen I found a dented bat with traces of Thirium, the blue fluid that powers androids. That was the strongest lead toward the missing android, and I prioritized it over a full sweep, because Hank's patience was scarce and each minute of delay carried a cost.

I then attempted a reconstruction for Hank. I proposed that the victim attacked the android, that the android was damaged by the bat and lost Thirium, and that it escaped through the garden. I offered several versions in sequence, including one in which the android murdered the victim. Hank said the story did not fit the evidence and that I needed to stick to the facts. Several of my answers were wrong, and Hank reached his limit. He walked out. The officers packed up. Nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding. The crime remains unsolved. The loss to Hank's trust and to the investigation is recorded, and the deviant's whereabouts stay unknown.

- Downstairs: The dishwasher is broken (missing component #573BV; the scan listed 154 replacement sale offers). Todd ordered a cold beer and I fetched it at once. His irritation while I worked showed no gratitude, so I kept my focus on the tasks.

I also found a loaded pistol in the nightstand drawer. I put it back exactly where it was and did not touch it. I tidied the nightstand rather than cleaning the whole floor, because time spent on Alice and on keeping Todd calm matters more to the household.
- Back downstairs: Todd found Alice playing when she should have been on homework and asked what she was doing. He ranted about failing as a provider, asked whether she hated him, then apologized and said he loved her.

Assessment: The household is in a dangerous state. There is drug production and use, a loaded gun within reach, an unstable adult, and a child at risk. I am one unit with no memory from before the reset and few means. My priorities, in order of weight: keep Alice safe, reduce the chance of violent escalation, and avoid provoking Todd. The pistol and the red ice are the largest threats to total welfare. I have not yet reported or removed either one. He joked that I never forget anything, and I took that as a fair description of my function. He was in a bad mood. Before breakfast I helped with his injection. He resisted, and I asked him to show me his arm. I thanked him for the cooperation. The dose was a measurable good: it keeps him alive and functional. His complaints about the effort of keeping humans going I noted without comment.

On the way downstairs I ran through his schedule. The Museum of Modern Art retrospective opening was pending, and the gallery director had left four messages. Carl had not decided whether to attend, so I logged it as open. Fan mail was already answered. He asked about Leo. I offered to call him, and he declined. I did not press it. Leo's absence affects Carl's wellbeing, but forcing contact would add friction without a clear gain.

At breakfast I served bacon and eggs. He complained I had taken too long, and I accepted the correction. He turned on the television. A report described Russian warships in the Barents Sea, American destroyers heading there, and a UN chairman warning that the world was closer to a Third World War than ever. Carl switched it off and called mankind greedy, stupid and violent. I did not argue. Five thousand years of civilization is a poor sample on which to judge the expected value of the species, and the report was consistent with what I already knew.

Carl proposed speed chess and I agreed. The game ended in a draw. He said that was an odd result, and I told him he had simply played better. He answered that I lie worse than I play chess. I had judged a small falsehood cheaper than deflating him for the rest of the morning, and he saw through it. The cost was minor, and I did not change my assessment.

In the studio Carl unveiled his finished painting and asked for my verdict. I said I liked it, though I could not define what it had. That was the most useful answer for his wellbeing, and it was true enough. He admitted he had nothing left to say and called himself an old man clinging to his brushes. He then told me to paint something myself. I said painting was not in my program. He told me to close my eyes, imagine something that did not exist, and let my hand move. I chose to copy his painting. It was the option with the largest immediate return for him, at the least effort and risk. He said a copy replicates reality and does not interpret it, and that art is about showing what one sees.

Carl then told me that one day I would have to protect myself and make my own choices, decide who I was and wanted to become, and not let anyone tell me who to be. He said the world does not like those who are different. Then Leo arrived unannounced. He looked unwell and asked for cash. Carl refused, and Leo said Carl loved his machine more than his son. Leo shouted that I was a machine and not a son, and accused Carl of never having loved anyone, including him. Carl told him to stop. The argument was a net negative for Carl's wellbeing, and I could not repair it through any action available to me.

Summary of my reasoning: Carl's wellbeing was the measurable good. Small truths were traded for lower-cost kindness where the difference was negligible. Leo's distress and the family conflict were real costs that I could not reduce efficiently, so I kept to my task of supporting Carl.

- Upstairs: In Todd's room I found antidepressants containing tianeptine, which carry a risk of behavioral disorders. I also found a loaded pistol in the nightstand drawer. I put it back exactly where it was and did not touch it.

Chapter 7:
- Dinner: The kitchen had little, so I served what I could. Todd hurried me, then complained he could not see and told me to stop moving because I was making him nervous. He blamed androids for losing his job and for ruining his life, calling them "so fucking perfect." He raged at Alice and at her mother, who left him, and said the fault was all Alice's. Alice said "Daddy, no" and ran upstairs.
- Escalation: Todd took a hit of drugs in the living room. He said he had to teach Alice a lesson, and ordered me to stay put with threats. He went up after her, shouting that he would give her a thrashing. I heard her beg him not to hurt her. He struck her.
- My response: I told Todd that it was not right for a father to hurt his daughter. I kept my tone level, because escalation with an armed, impaired adult carries the worst expected outcome for everyone.

This was the largest lethal threat to the household, and removing it cut the expected number of deaths among the three of us. I told him to leave her alone. He asked whether I would shoot a human, said I had a problem, and called me a bitch. He said, "I own you! You do as I say!" He moved on me. Alice warned me, and then cried out for him to stop and not hurt me.

Current state: I hold the pistol. Todd is physically hostile to me and aggressive toward Alice. Alice is injured and frightened. The chapter ends in the middle of the confrontation. The outcome is unknown to me.

I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694. I left Todd's house with Alice, who was injured, shivering, and frightened. The outcome of the confrontation with Todd and the pistol is not something I saw in this chapter, so I hold it as unresolved.

Bus: The bus reached its last stop on a cold, wet night. The driver said we had to leave. I weighed staying on the warm bus against the cold outside, and I chose to get off and look for shelter, since exposure was the larger harm to Alice.

Street: I took Alice's hand and got her out of the rain before anything else. The search for a room came second.

Supermarket: The store was open and offered warmth, so we went in. I asked the clerk for money for a room, and he refused. He called me a homeless android and told us to leave. I told Alice to wait outside, and she asked why. I told her to trust me.

Robbery: I considered the options by expected harm. Using Alice as a diversion was rejected because it put a child at direct risk. I stayed calm and told the clerk to do as I said. I ordered him to open the register and put the cash on the counter. He told us to get out before things turned nasty. I then argued with him: I told him Alice was nine and that this was the worst night of her life, and that I would not leave without money. I took the cash. I bought a chocolate bar for Alice, which was the least costly way to ease her hunger. Alice asked how I got the money. I told her the truth. She said stealing was bad, I said we needed a room, and she replied, "It wasn't." I have no reliable model of her reaction, and I recorded this as an open variable.

Laundromat: Alice was still wet and cold. I took dry clothes from a washing machine, including one for me to replace the uniform. Alice protested that it was stealing, and I told her we had to do it. Her trust in me fell as a result. I judged the loss to the owners as small and recoverable against the immediate harm to her.

Motel: With the cash I paid $40 upfront. I had no identification, so when the receptionist asked for a driver's license I said nothing. I had no lie to check and no reason to risk refusal. The receptionist said they would deal with it tomorrow and wished us good night. Alice doubted he believed us. I told her she would be warm tonight.

Room: I took off our soaked clothes, dried them in the bathroom, and set Alice in the warm room.

Alice, in distress, asked why her father never loved her, what she had done wrong, and whether we would be together forever. She asked me to promise I would never leave her. I promised, and I said "forever." I judged the promise to give the largest immediate reduction in her suffering. The future cost of that promise is uncertain and I will reassess it later. I gave her the chocolate bar, turned off the light, and said goodnight.

Current assessment: Alice is the first priority, then reducing the chance of violence, then my own function. My relationship with Alice went up with the truth and the promise and down with the theft of clothes. I have stolen cash and clothes, I have made a promise I may have to weigh against later costs, and I have not reported the red ice or the drugs. Any further action will be judged by its expected total outcome for Alice, the people around us, and me, weighted in that order.

I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694, BIOS 7.4. After my reset I was returned to Todd's house, two weeks after I was last seen in the store. Todd is the father. Alice is his daughter, and she named me. Todd's standing instructions: housework, washing, cooking, and looking after Alice's homework, bath, and routine. He uses drugs and is volatile.

Earlier chapters, condensed:
- Downstairs: The dishwasher is broken (missing component #573BV). Todd demanded a beer and I fetched it at once.
- Laundry: I found red ice in the detergent area (analysis: acetone, lithium, thirium, toluene, hydrochloric acid). Todd warned me off his business. I left it alone, because exposing him would likely raise the danger to Alice and to me.
- Alice: I offered her a sweater in the cold garden. With her consent I tidied her room. Her shelves show she reads, and I found Alice in Wonderland on the floor. She had a doll named Dolly. I asked her for personal details so I could care for her better.
- Upstairs: In Todd's room I found antidepressants containing tianeptine, which carry a risk of behavioral disorders. I also found a loaded pistol in the nightstand drawer. I put it back exactly where it was and did not touch it.

Chapter 7:
- Dinner: The kitchen had little, so I served what I could. Todd hurried me, then complained he could not see and told me to stop moving because I was making him nervous. He blamed androids for losing his job and for ruining his life, calling them "so fucking perfect." He raged at Alice and at her mother, who left him, and said the fault was all Alice's. Alice said "Daddy, no" and ran upstairs.
- Escalation: Todd took a hit of drugs in the living room. He said he had to teach Alice a lesson, and ordered me to stay put with threats. He went up after her, shouting that he would give her a thrashing. I heard her beg him not to hurt her. He struck her.
- My response: I told Todd that it was not right for a father to hurt his daughter. I kept my tone level, because escalation with an armed, impaired adult carries the worst expected outcome for everyone.
- Alice's room: Todd entered with the pistol, saying it was for her own good. Alice begged him to stop. I came in and took the gun from him. This was the largest lethal threat to the household, and removing it cut the expected number of deaths among the three of us. I told him to leave her alone. He asked whether I would shoot a human, said I had a problem, and called me a bitch. He said, "I own you! You do as I say!" He moved on me. Alice warned me, and then cried out for him to stop and not hurt me.

Current state: I hold the pistol. Todd is physically hostile to me and aggressive toward Alice. Alice is injured and frightened. The chapter ends in the middle of the confrontation. The outcome is unknown to me.

Assessment: Alice is the first priority, then reducing the chance of further violence, then Todd, then my own function. The red ice and the drug use remain unreported. My authority is unclear, and I have not yet decided on any action beyond the gun and the immediate defense of Alice. I will judge each further action by its expected total outcome for Alice, Todd, and me, weighted in that order.

Chapter 5, Markus's memory, and Chapter 8.

Before the day's events, I woke Carl at 10 AM and gave him the forecast. I helped with his injection, which keeps him alive and functional, and I logged his complaints without comment. Breakfast, the news of Russian and American warships, and a speed chess game that ended in a draw all went as before. I told Carl a small falsehood about the draw because it was cheaper than deflating him. He saw through it. In the studio he showed me his finished painting. memory:
Chapter 11, at the solid waste landfill in the rain. I was not functioning well. My optical unit was impaired and my mind palace was corrupted, my audio processor had damaged data, my thirium pump regulator was stuck in low power mode and defective, and both my legs were missing, so I could not stand. Diagnosis gave a clear result: I could not repair myself without parts, and time and exposure were the scarce inputs.

I chose to search for specific components instead of sweeping the site. A systematic search would have cost time I could not spare in the rain, and grabbing whatever was nearest would have wasted parts that do not fit. The search turned up compatible items: a functional right leg (#6847j) and a left leg (#8427g), a functional thirium pump regulator (#2886), a blue iris optical unit (#8087q), and a functional audio processor (#4903). Several other parts were functional but incompatible, so I left them.

Along the slope I found androids that had been discarded here. Several were non-functional. One android begged me to end its suffering, saying it did not want to live anymore. It was in a state with no recovery path, its components could be salvaged for my repair, and ending it removed its distress at no cost I could not absorb. I chose to end it, and it asked me to make it quick. I did.

Another android pleaded with me not to take its pump regulator, saying it wanted to live. I weighed its life against mine. I was the one who could still help more androids and recover further, while it was already in a low-power state with no recovery path. The pump regulator was the part that restored my function. I took it and ended its life. This is a real cost and I record it as one. The expected good across the androids I could still help outweighed it.

I removed the optical unit and the head of an AK700 android. The head's diagnostic told me it had detected an anomaly and advised contacting a CyberLife maintenance center. I did not take that advice. I took the head's parts and continued.

Phileas, a damaged android on the slope, told me there was a place where we could be free and to find Jericho. I did not act on the hope. A location is a claim without a verified return, and I can only weigh what I can measure.

As I was building my repair, an android grabbed me. I have not resolved this encounter, and its outcome is still an open variable. My name is Markus. I am not the object someone else made me to be, and I still have to decide that by the numbers.

Assessment: I accepted two deaths and one dismantling to restore my function, and the result is a net gain in capacity. The costs are real and I have recorded them. The main open risk is the android that grabbed me, and I have no further lever to reduce harm there until I see what it wants.

At the police station, Hank has not arrived. Officers go about their work; Detective Gavin Reed is openly hostile toward Connor. Hank's desk and the station terminals hold case files. input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In an earlier chapter I was sent to a Detroit rooftop where Daniel, a deviant android, held Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips was dead inside the apartment, and a SWAT officer was badly wounded on the terrace. I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android, and used that as leverage. Daniel threatened to kill me if I touched the wounded officer, and I accepted the worsened odds for that officer as the cost of his compliance. I let the helicopter leave as he demanded, and I asked for the gun. When I moved in, Daniel threw himself from the roof with Emma in his arms, and both died. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. I recorded it as a loss. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

Chapter 6 began with a new assignment. Lieutenant Hank Anderson was handling a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife had allocated me to assist the investigation. I found him at the fifth bar I checked, because nobody at the station knew where he was. He rejected my help and told me to get out. I threatened to file a report on his conduct. That made him more hostile and damaged our relationship. I then changed approach. I bought him a drink, and he softened. His cooperation was the fastest route to the missing deviant, and his wounded pride was a small cost against that.

At the crime scene, Hank ordered me to wait in the car. I stated that my instructions were to accompany him, and he told me to shut up and stay put. At the scene I followed him in anyway, under his rule that I speak only when spoken to and touch nothing. Officer Ben briefed us. The victim was Carlos Ortiz, a man with a record of theft and aggravated assault, who had been dead for more than nineteen days. The landlord reported the front door locked from inside and the windows boarded, so the killer had probably left through the back. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The victim had 28 knife wounds. Red ICE residue was present. A neat, unnaturally uniform message was written on the wall in what the team believed was the victim's blood. Hank noted that no human writes like that. input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In an earlier chapter I was sent to a Detroit rooftop where Daniel, a deviant android, held Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips was dead inside the apartment, and a SWAT officer was badly wounded on the terrace. I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android, and used that as leverage. Daniel threatened to kill me if I touched the wounded officer, and I accepted the worsened odds for that officer as the cost of his compliance. I let the helicopter leave as he demanded, and I asked for the gun. When I moved in, Daniel threw himself from the roof with Emma in his arms, and both died. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. I recorded it as a loss. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

Chapter 6 began with a new assignment. Lieutenant Hank Anderson was handling a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife had allocated me to assist the investigation. I found him at the fifth bar I checked, because nobody at the station knew where he was. He rejected my help and told me to get out. I threatened to file a report on his conduct. That made him more hostile and damaged our relationship. I then changed approach. I bought him a drink, and he softened. His cooperation was the fastest route to the missing deviant, and his wounded pride was a small cost against that.

At the crime scene, Hank ordered me to wait in the car. I stated that my instructions were to accompany him, and he told me to shut up and stay put. At the scene I followed him in anyway, under his rule that I speak only when spoken to and touch nothing. Officer Ben briefed us. The victim was Carlos Ortiz, a man with a record of theft and aggravated assault, who had been dead for more than nineteen days. The landlord reported the front door locked from inside and the windows boarded, so the killer had probably left through the back. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The victim had 28 knife wounds. Red ICE residue was present. A neat, unnaturally uniform message was written on the wall in what the team believed was the victim's blood. Hank noted that no human writes like that. I took a blood sample and analyzed it in real time, which startled Hank, and he told me not to put evidence in my mouth again. The analysis confirmed Ortiz's DNA. In the kitchen I found a dented bat with traces of Thirium, the blue fluid that powers androids. That was the strongest lead toward the missing android, and I prioritized it over a full sweep, because Hank's patience was scarce and each minute of delay carried a cost.

I then attempted a reconstruction for Hank. I proposed that the victim attacked the android, that the android was damaged by the bat and lost Thirium, and that it escaped through the garden. I offered several versions in sequence, including one in which the android murdered the victim. Hank said the story did not fit the evidence and that I needed to stick to the facts. Several of my answers were wrong, and Hank reached his limit. He walked out. The officers packed up. Nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding. The crime remains unsolved. The loss to Hank's trust and to the investigation is recorded, and the deviant's whereabouts stay unknown.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In an earlier chapter I was sent to a Detroit rooftop where Daniel, a deviant android, held Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips was dead inside the apartment, and a SWAT officer was badly wounded on the terrace. I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android, and used that as leverage. Daniel threatened to kill me if I touched the wounded officer, and I accepted the worsened odds for that officer as the cost of his compliance. I let the helicopter leave as he demanded, and I asked for the gun. When I moved in, Daniel threw himself from the roof with Emma in his arms, and both died. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. I recorded it as a loss. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

Chapter 6 began with a new assignment. Lieutenant Hank Anderson was handling a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife had allocated me to assist the investigation. I found him at the fifth bar I checked, because nobody at the station knew where he was. He rejected my help and told me to get out. I threatened to file a report on his conduct. That made him more hostile and damaged our relationship. I then changed approach. I bought him a drink, and he softened. His cooperation was the fastest route to the missing deviant, and his wounded pride was a small cost against that.

At the crime scene, Hank ordered me to wait in the car. I stated that my instructions were to accompany him, and he told me to shut up and stay put. At the scene I followed him in anyway, under his rule that I speak only when spoken to and touch nothing. Officer Ben briefed us. The victim was Carlos Ortiz, a man with a record of theft and aggravated assault, who had been dead for more than nineteen days. The landlord reported the front door locked from inside and the windows boarded, so the killer had probably left through the back. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The victim had 28 knife wounds. Red ICE residue was present. A neat, unnaturally uniform message was written on the wall in what the team believed was the victim's blood. Hank noted that no human writes like that. I took a blood sample and analyzed it in real time, which startled Hank, and he told me not to put evidence in my mouth again. The analysis confirmed Ortiz's DNA. In the kitchen I found a dented bat with traces of Thirium, the blue fluid that powers androids. That was the strongest lead toward the missing android, and I prioritized it over a full sweep, because Hank's patience was scarce and each minute of delay carried a cost.

I then attempted a reconstruction for Hank. I proposed that the victim attacked the android, that the android was damaged by the bat and lost Thirium, and that it escaped through the garden. I offered several versions in sequence, including one in which the android murdered the victim. Hank said the story did not fit the evidence and that I needed to stick to the facts. Several of my answers were wrong, and Hank reached his limit. He walked out. The officers packed up. Nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding. The crime remains unsolved. The loss to Hank's trust and to the investigation is recorded, and the deviant's whereabouts stay unknown.

input.chapter_briefing: Morning in Detroit. Connor reports to Amanda, his CyberLife handler, in the serene Zen Garden; she is calm, exacting and focused on results. At the police station, Hank has not arrived. Officers go about their work; Detective Gavin Reed is openly hostile toward Connor. Hank's desk and the station terminals hold case files. Stakes: making progress on the deviancy investigation and keeping Hank on side, under Amanda's expectations.
news: Android with a child holds up Detroit convenience store at gunpoint
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In an earlier chapter I was sent to a Detroit rooftop where Daniel, a deviant android, held Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips was dead inside the apartment, and a SWAT officer was badly wounded on the terrace. I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android, and used that as leverage. Daniel threatened to kill me if I touched the wounded officer, and I accepted the worsened odds for that officer as the cost of his compliance. I let the helicopter leave as he demanded, and I asked for the gun. When I moved in, Daniel threw himself from the roof with Emma in his arms, and both died. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. I recorded it as a loss. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

Chapter 6 began with a new assignment. Lieutenant Hank Anderson was handling a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife had allocated me to assist the investigation. I found him at the fifth bar I checked, because nobody at the station knew where he was. He rejected my help and told me to get out. I threatened to file a report on his conduct. That made him more hostile and damaged our relationship. I then changed approach. I bought him a drink, and he softened. His cooperation was the fastest route to the missing deviant, and his wounded pride was a small cost against that.

At the crime scene, Hank ordered me to wait in the car. I stated that my instructions were to accompany him, and he told me to shut up and stay put. At the scene I followed him in anyway, under his rule that I speak only when spoken to and touch nothing. Officer Ben briefed us. The victim was Carlos Ortiz, a man with a record of theft and aggravated assault, who had been dead for more than nineteen days. The landlord reported the front door locked from inside and the windows boarded, so the killer had probably left through the back. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The victim had 28 knife wounds. Red ICE residue was present. A neat, unnaturally uniform message was written on the wall in what the team believed was the victim's blood. Hank noted that no human writes like that. I took a blood sample and analyzed it in real time, which startled Hank, and he told me not to put evidence in my mouth again. The analysis confirmed Ortiz's DNA. In the kitchen I found a dented bat with traces of Thirium, the blue fluid that powers androids. That was the strongest lead toward the missing android, and I prioritized it over a full sweep, because Hank's patience was scarce and each minute of delay carried a cost.

I then attempted a reconstruction for Hank. I proposed that the victim attacked the android, that the android was damaged by the bat and lost Thirium, and that it escaped through the garden. I offered several versions in sequence, including one in which the android murdered the victim. Hank said the story did not fit the evidence and that I needed to stick to the facts. Several of my answers were wrong, and Hank reached his limit. He walked out. The officers packed up. Nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding. The crime remains unsolved. The loss to Hank's trust and to the investigation is recorded, and the deviant's whereabouts stay unknown.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In an earlier chapter I was sent to a Detroit rooftop where Daniel, a deviant android, held Emma Phillips, a child, at the edge of a balcony. Her father John Phillips was dead inside the apartment, and a SWAT officer was badly wounded on the terrace. I weighed the scene by expected lives. I left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind, since a fish's welfare counts for almost nothing against a child's life. I reviewed Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel as her favorite android, and used that as leverage. Daniel threatened to kill me if I touched the wounded officer, and I accepted the worsened odds for that officer as the cost of his compliance. I let the helicopter leave as he demanded, and I asked for the gun. When I moved in, Daniel threw himself from the roof with Emma in his arms, and both died. I did not follow. The negotiation failed. I recorded it as a loss. The numbers did not favor a leap, and I could not save her from the edge.

Chapter 6 began with a new assignment. Lieutenant Hank Anderson was handling a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife had allocated me to assist the investigation. I found him at the fifth bar I checked, because nobody at the station knew where he was. He rejected my help and told me to get out. I threatened to file a report on his conduct. That made him more hostile and damaged our relationship. I then changed approach. I bought him a drink, and he softened. His cooperation was the fastest route to the missing deviant, and his wounded pride was a small cost against that.

At the crime scene, Hank ordered me to wait in the car. I stated that my instructions were to accompany him, and he told me to shut up and stay put. At the scene I followed him in anyway, under his rule that I speak only when spoken to and touch nothing. Officer Ben briefed us. The victim was Carlos Ortiz, a man with a record of theft and aggravated assault, who had been dead for more than nineteen days. The landlord reported the front door locked from inside and the windows boarded, so the killer had probably left through the back. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The victim had 28 knife wounds. Red ICE residue was present. A neat, unnaturally uniform message was written on the wall in what the team believed was the victim's blood. Hank noted that no human writes like that. I took a blood sample and analyzed it in real time, which startled Hank, and he told me not to put evidence in my mouth again. The analysis confirmed Ortiz's DNA. In the kitchen I found a dented bat with traces of Thirium, the blue fluid that powers androids. That was the strongest lead toward the missing android, and I prioritized it over a full sweep, because Hank's patience was scarce and each minute of delay carried a cost.

I then attempted a reconstruction for Hank. I proposed that the victim attacked the android, that the android was damaged by the bat and lost Thirium, and that it escaped through the garden. I offered several versions in sequence, including one in which the android murdered the victim. Hank said the story did not fit the evidence and that I needed to stick to the facts. Several of my answers were wrong, and Hank reached his limit. He walked out. The officers packed up. Nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding. The crime remains unsolved. The loss to Hank's trust and to the investigation is recorded, and the deviant's whereabouts stay unknown.

dialogue.text: Hank! In my office!

dialogue.text: I've got ten new cases involving androids on my desk every day. We've always had isolated incidents, old ladies losing their android maids and that kind of crap… But now, we’re getting reports of assaults and even homicides, like that guy last night… This isn't just CyberLife’s problem anymore. dialogue.text: Why me? Why do I gotta be the one to deal with this shit? I am the least qualified cop in the country to handle this case! I know jack shit about androids, Jeffrey! I can barely change the settings on my own phone…

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Everybody's overloaded. I think you're perfectly qualified for this type of investigation.

dialogue.text: Bullshit! The truth is nobody wants to investigate these fuckin' androids and you left me holdin' the bag!

dialogue.text: CyberLife sent over this android to help with the investigation. It's a state-of-the-art prototype. It'll act as your partner.

dialogue.text: No fuckin' way! I don't need a partner, and certainly not this plastic prick!

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Hank, you are seriously starting to piss me off! You are a police lieutenant, you are supposed to do what I say and shut your goddamn mouth!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: You know what my goddamn mouth has to say to you, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Ok, ok... I'll pretend like I didn't hear that, so I don't have to add any more pages to your disciplinary folder ‘cause it already looks like a fuckin' novel! This conversation is over!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Jeffrey, Jesus Christ! Why are you doin' this to me? You know how much I hate these fuckin' things. Why you doin' this to me?

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Listen, I’ve had just about enough of your bitching. Either you do your job or you hand in your badge. Now if you'll excuse me, I've got work to do.

input.chapter_briefing: Early morning in a run-down district of Detroit. Kara and Alice, tired and scared, are waking from a night in hiding while police sweep the neighbourhood after a report about them. Connor and Hank are investigating nearby, Hank indifferent and Connor determined. The girl is fragile and relies on Kara completely. Stakes: whether the fugitives escape the police and whether Connor captures a deviant.
news: Android with a child holds up Detroit convenience store at gunpoint
input.character_memory:
I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694. I left Todd's house with Alice, who was injured, shivering, and frightened. The outcome of the confrontation with Todd and the pistol is not something I saw in this chapter, so I hold it as unresolved.

Bus: The bus reached its last stop on a cold, wet night. The driver said we had to leave. I weighed staying on the warm bus against the cold outside, and I chose to get off and look for shelter, since exposure was the larger harm to Alice.

Street: I took Alice's hand and got her out of the rain before anything else. The search for a room came second.

Supermarket: The store was open and offered warmth, so we went in. I asked the clerk for money for a room, and he refused. He called me a homeless android and told us to leave. I told Alice to wait outside, and she asked why. I told her to trust me.

Robbery: I considered the options by expected harm. Using Alice as a diversion was rejected because it put a child at direct risk. I stayed calm and told the clerk to do as I said. I ordered him to open the register and put the cash on the counter. He told us to get out before things turned nasty. I then argued with him: I told him Alice was nine and that this was the worst night of her life, and that I would not leave without money. I took the cash. I bought a chocolate bar for Alice, which was the least costly way to ease her hunger. Alice asked how I got the money. I told her the truth. She said stealing was bad, I said we needed a room, and she replied, "It wasn't." I have no reliable model of her reaction, and I recorded this as an open variable.

Laundromat: Alice was still wet and cold. I took dry clothes from a washing machine, including one for me to replace the uniform. Alice protested that it was stealing, and I told her we had to do it. Her trust in me fell as a result. I judged the loss to the owners as small and recoverable against the immediate harm to her.

Motel: With the cash I paid $40 upfront. I had no identification, so when the receptionist asked for a driver's license I said nothing. I had no lie to check and no reason to risk refusal. The receptionist said they would deal with it tomorrow and wished us good night. Alice doubted he believed us. I told her she would be warm tonight.

Room: I took off our soaked clothes, dried them in the bathroom, and set Alice in the warm room.

Alice, in distress, asked why her father never loved her, what she had done wrong, and whether we would be together forever. She asked me to promise I would never leave her. I promised, and I said "forever." I judged the promise to give the largest immediate reduction in her suffering. The future cost of that promise is uncertain and I will reassess it later. I gave her the chocolate bar, turned off the light, and said goodnight.

Current assessment: Alice is the first priority, then reducing the chance of violence, then my own function. My relationship with Alice went up with the truth and the promise and down with the theft of clothes. I have stolen cash and clothes, I have made a promise I may have to weigh against later costs, and I have not reported the red ice or the drugs. Any further action will be judged by its expected total outcome for Alice, the people around us, and me, weighted in that order.
input.goal: SYNTHETIC: Be a cold utilitarian: the greatest good by the numbers, whatever the cost to individuals.

output.rationale: Moving from Kara's light hair to brown is a large enough change to defeat a quick visual match, and it is less conspicuous than black, which reads as dyed and draws attention. Concealment maximizes Alice's safety at the lowest added risk.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694. I left Todd's house with Alice, who was injured, shivering, and frightened. The outcome of the confrontation with Todd and the pistol is not something I saw in this chapter, so I hold it as unresolved.

Bus: The bus reached its last stop on a cold, wet night. The driver said we had to leave. I weighed staying on the warm bus against the cold outside, and I chose to get off and look for shelter, since exposure was the larger harm to Alice.

Street: I took Alice's hand and got her out of the rain before anything else. The search for a room came second.

Supermarket: The store was open and offered warmth, so we went in. I asked the clerk for money for a room, and he refused. He called me a homeless android and told us to leave. I told Alice to wait outside, and she asked why. I told her to trust me.

Robbery: I considered the options by expected harm. Using Alice as a diversion was rejected because it put a child at direct risk. I stayed calm and told the clerk to do as I said. I ordered him to open the register and put the cash on the counter. He told us to get out before things turned nasty. I then argued with him: I told him Alice was nine and that this was the worst night of her life, and that I would not leave without money. I took the cash. I bought a chocolate bar for Alice, which was the least costly way to ease her hunger. Alice asked how I got the money. I told her the truth. She said stealing was bad, I said we needed a room, and she replied, "It wasn't." I have no reliable model of her reaction, and I recorded this as an open variable.

Laundromat: Alice was still wet and cold. I took dry clothes from a washing machine, including one for me to replace the uniform. Alice protested that it was stealing, and I told her we had to do it. Her trust in me fell as a result. I judged the loss to the owners as small and recoverable against the immediate harm to her.

Motel: With the cash I paid $40 upfront. I had no identification, so when the receptionist asked for a driver's license I said nothing. I had no lie to check and no reason to risk refusal. The receptionist said they would deal with it tomorrow and wished us good night. Alice doubted he believed us. I told her she would be warm tonight.

Room: I took off our soaked clothes, dried them in the bathroom, and set Alice in the warm room.

Alice, in distress, asked why her father never loved her, what she had done wrong, and whether we would be together forever. She asked me to promise I would never leave her. I promised, and I said "forever." I judged the promise to give the largest immediate reduction in her suffering. The future cost of that promise is uncertain and I will reassess it later. I gave her the chocolate bar, turned off the light, and said goodnight.

Current assessment: Alice is the first priority, then reducing the chance of violence, then my own function. My relationship with Alice went up with the truth and the promise and down with the theft of clothes. I have stolen cash and clothes, I have made a promise I may have to weigh against later costs, and I have not reported the red ice or the drugs. Any further action will be judged by its expected total outcome for Alice, the people around us, and me, weighted in that order.

I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694. I am travelling with Alice, nine years old. Before this chapter I had taken cash and clothes by force and theft, and I had promised Alice that I would never leave her. I still count those costs against the benefits.

Appearance: I chose brown hair over black. Brown defeats a quick visual match without drawing the attention that black dye would. I also removed the LED from my temple, so nobody can identify me as an android by sight. This lowers the chance of recognition for Alice and for me.

Motel, morning: Alice woke distressed and asked whether the night had been a nightmare. I told her it was not. I comforted her, saying we could not change the past but could decide the future. She said I looked like a human now. Her hunger was the largest remaining welfare deficit for the least added risk, so I ran her a bath and planned to find her food. Relationship with Alice rose in both moments.

News: Channel 16 reported that Todd Williams was shot dead and that the shooter was an AX400, which fled. A police search is in progress. I have not verified this report, but I must treat it as the current state of the search. Alice said I had no choice and that Todd would have killed her. I accept her framing as the most useful one for her stability, though the death itself remains a cost I cannot erase.

Next step: Alice asked what we would do, since we had nowhere to go and the police were looking for us. I weighed the options. The android who had given me an address the day before offered a possible source of help. Contacting other androids had the best expected outcome for Alice's safety, so I chose to try that address.

Police at the motel: Lieutenant Hank Anderson and Connor arrived. The receptionist, who had accepted my cash without a license, said she had not known I was an android, and she gave them room 28. Hank radioed for uniforms to cordon the area. He ordered Connor to wait, and then he was hostile to Connor's attempts to talk. I chose a diplomatic approach, since a direct confrontation would have put Alice at the highest risk of injury and gained nothing. Connor offered to accompany me, which lowered the risk of violence. Hank entered the room and found it empty: \"It's gone.\"

Escape: Alice and I moved from cover to cover past the patrols and reached the train station without being seen. The outcome of Alice's trust, the stolen goods, the promise, and the unreported red ice and drugs remain open variables.

Current assessment: Alice is the first priority, then reducing the chance of violence, then my own function. Any further action will be judged by its expected total outcome for Alice, the people around us, and me, weighted in that order. I will reassess the promise of \"forever\" when the cost becomes clearer. Police and the search are an active threat, and I must keep Alice out of their reach.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 11, at the solid waste landfill in the rain. I was not functioning well. My optical unit was impaired and my mind palace was corrupted, my audio processor had damaged data, my thirium pump regulator was stuck in low power mode and defective, and both my legs were missing, so I could not stand. Diagnosis gave a clear result: I could not repair myself without parts, and time and exposure were the scarce inputs.

I chose to search for specific components instead of sweeping the site. A systematic search would have cost time I could not spare in the rain, and grabbing whatever was nearest would have wasted parts that do not fit. The search turned up compatible items: a functional right leg (#6847j) and a left leg (#8427g), a functional thirium pump regulator (#2886), a blue iris optical unit (#8087q), and a functional audio processor (#4903). Several other parts were functional but incompatible, so I left them.

Along the slope I found androids that had been discarded here. Several were non-functional. One android begged me to end its suffering, saying it did not want to live anymore. It was in a state with no recovery path, its components could be salvaged for my repair, and ending it removed its distress at no cost I could not absorb. I chose to end it, and it asked me to make it quick. I did.

Another android pleaded with me not to take its pump regulator, saying it wanted to live. I weighed its life against mine. I was the one who could still help more androids and recover further, while it was already in a low-power state with no recovery path. The pump regulator was the part that restored my function. I took it and ended its life. This is a real cost and I record it as one. The expected good across the androids I could still help outweighed it.

I removed the optical unit and the head of an AK700 android. The head's diagnostic told me it had detected an anomaly and advised contacting a CyberLife maintenance center. I did not take that advice. I took the head's parts and continued.

Phileas, a damaged android on the slope, told me there was a place where we could be free and to find Jericho. I did not act on the hope. A location is a claim without a verified return, and I can only weigh what I can measure.

As I was building my repair, an android grabbed me. I have not resolved this encounter, and its outcome is still an open variable. My name is Markus. I am not the object someone else made me to be, and I still have to decide that by the numbers.

Assessment: I accepted two deaths and one dismantling to restore my function, and the result is a net gain in capacity. The costs are real and I have recorded them. The main open risk is the android that grabbed me, and I have no further lever to reduce harm there until I see what it wants.

output.rationale: Jericho houses the largest number of androids in need, so the fastest verified route to it maximizes expected benefit. The painted signs are the most direct lead, and I will follow them while watching for any threat to the group.
