dialogue.text: There's a spare room upstairs. You can put her to bed and I'll bring her something to eat. Adam, will you show them upstairs?

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I'm fine, Kara… We can't stop because of me.  We've got to get across the border…

chapter_segment.rationale: Rose can only help Alice's fever and plan the crossing well if she has accurate facts, so explaining our situation gives the best expected outcome for Alice and the others. Reassurance without substance risks a bad plan, and silence leaves the most important risk unmanaged.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Don’t worry Alice, these people are going to help us. Get some rest, and this time tomorrow, we’ll be in Canada. I promise.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Why do humans hate us? We didn’t do anything wrong…

chapter_segment.rationale: Rose's help depends on an accurate picture of our situation, so a measured, nuanced answer gives the best expected outcome for Alice and the others. It avoids both emotional overstatement and a misleading simplification that could cost us the route north.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Humans are...  Complicated. Sometimes it’s difficult to understand them.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Why can’t we just talk to each other? They’d see we’re not bad…

chapter_segment.rationale: Rose's network can only plan the fever care and the crossing well with accurate facts, and that serves the largest number of people, including the other androids it moves. Telling her the truth carries a bounded risk, while a false or overly hopeful picture would raise the expected cost to Alice and everyone depending on this route.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I don’t know… I really don’t know…

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: I don't know what you like but I made you Rose’s world famous spaghetti. You’ll be back on your feet in no time.  There's something for her fever.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: I'll get these washed and dried.

chapter_segment.rationale: Alice has a fever and has refused food, and nourishment is the cheapest measurable way to raise her odds of recovery before the crossing. Encouraging her to eat costs almost nothing and serves the greatest expected welfare, so it outweighs a goodnight kiss or leaving her.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: You need to eat something. You haven't had anything since we left… Promise me you'll try?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I'll be downstairs if you need anything.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Get some sleep... And tomorrow, you’ll be stronger than me! I'll stay with her a while.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: I didn't get your name…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I'm Kara.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: This is my son, Adam. I'm Rose, but you know that already… Come and have a seat, Kara. So, are you gonna tell me what a deviant’s doing in the snow with a little girl?

chapter_segment.rationale: Rose's network can only plan Alice's fever care and the crossing well with accurate facts, and that serves the most people, including the androids it moves. A guarded answer keeps the risk of misplanning in place without lowering the expected cost to Alice.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Her father was beating her. When I saw what was happening…  Something snapped inside of me. All of a sudden, I felt like her life was more important than mine. I had to protect her... So we ran away.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: I understand…

chapter_segment.rationale: Rose's network is only worth the risk if it moves many androids, so I want the actual numbers before I weigh Alice's safety against the cost to Rose's household. Asking how many deviants she has moved gives me the figure I need to judge the expected benefit of trusting her.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We're not the first ones to come here.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: These past few weeks we’ve seen... More, and more… I don’t know what’s going on… But something’s happening…

chapter_segment.rationale: Rose's network has moved many androids, and Alice needs warmth and rest before the crossing, so the expected total benefit favours moving on inside the house. The DANGEROUS option adds risk to Alice and the household without a clear gain I can measure.

The only available option is BORDER, and the crossing is the sole route that serves the greatest expected good for Alice and the other androids. Remaining in the house with an unverified host carries costs I cannot yet quantify, so I accept the route.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We've heard you help androids cross the border.  Can you help us?

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: The only way is over the river and it's mostly frozen in winter. It's very risky. And after that android's speech on TV? Everybody’s on edge… It's probably safer for you to stay here until things settle down…

chapter_segment.rationale: Rose's household carries the risk if we press her to act against her judgement, and Alice needs rest before any crossing. Accepting her advice to wait for things to settle gives the lowest expected harm to the people involved.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We can't keep hiding like this… Alice needs to feel safe and have a normal life… We have to get across that border. No matter what. Please…  You've got to help us.

dialogue.speaker: Android 1
dialogue.text: Rose, come quickly!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: What's going on?

dialogue.speaker: Android 2
dialogue.text: It's Mary.  She just shut down…

dialogue.speaker: Android 3
dialogue.text: We escaped together…  We used to talk about what we would do once we got across the border…  I loved her.  I loved her more than anything.  What would I do without her?..

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Let's let them be…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Alice? What are you doing here? You should be resting…

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I wasn't sleepy…

chapter_segment.rationale: Alice has a fever and the temperature is dropping toward 22 degrees, so taking her out into the snow would sharply raise the expected harm to her. Staying gives her warmth, food and rest, and keeps the route through Rose's network open for everyone it serves.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Come on, Alice.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: She didn't wanna stay in her room any longer… You alright, Kara?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Yes...  I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: We can't hide them! Not after what those deviants did today! It's too dangerous! Do you know what'll happen if the police find them here? We'll go to prison, Mom! Do you understand me? Prison!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Adam, we’ve already talked about this!

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: No! I won't back down this time! You're gonna ruin our lives, and for what? For a bunch of machines?

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: They're not machines! They're alive!

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: I'm alive! You are alive! They!.. They're nothing! And none of this would be happening if dad was still here!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: I will not stand for that kind of talk!

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: I'm not going to prison because you wanna help these freaks!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: THAT IS ENOUGH ADAM! THAT'S ENOUGH!

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Don’t mind him… Sometimes he just boils over… It’s been hard since his dad passed away… But he's a fine boy!.. I'll go see about getting you across the border tonight, okay?.. You stay here, I won't be long.

chapter_segment.rationale: Alice has a fever and the temperature is falling, so every unnecessary movement adds risk to the person with the most at stake. Rose is the only known route north, and waiting for her keeps us warm and out of sight while the expected cost of searching the house is greater than its benefit.

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: The police!.. It's the police!

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: What are we gonna do? They know we're here!  We have to open the door! I knew this was gonna happen! I knew it!

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Hurry, Luther! Take Alice and hide…

chapter_segment.rationale: Alice has a fever and the temperature is falling, so getting her warm and resting in the spare room upstairs gives the best expected outcome for her and keeps us out of sight while Rose works on the crossing. Going upstairs also keeps Adam's hostility at a distance, which lowers the risk to the household.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: …upstairs!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Come on, Alice!

chapter_segment.rationale: Adam is the one person in this house who can expose us, and a threat would raise the odds of a call to the police, which endangers Alice, Rose's network and the household. Reassuring him that we will leave soon lowers the expected harm at the least cost.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Just keep calm, Adam, and everything will be alright.

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Good evening, Ma'am. Sorry to disturb you. We've had reports of androids in the area.  With all this deviant business going on, you can’t be too careful. Do you mind if I ask you a few questions? May I come in?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: 'Evening, young man.

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: Good evening…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Would you like a cup of coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: I'd love one. Have you noticed anything unusual recently? Any unexpected visitors?

chapter_segment.rationale: The policeman is already wandering the room, and Alice and Luther are hidden in the house. Staying with him lets me watch where he goes and control what he sees, which lowers the expected risk to Alice, Luther and the household more than leaving him unobserved to make coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: No… No, nothing in particular…

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Is anyone else in the house?

chapter_segment.rationale: Weighing the numbers, the policeman's visit threatens Alice, Luther, Rose's household and the wider network alike, so no single life should be favoured at the expense of the others. Choosing NOBODY keeps the expected harm spread across everyone in the house rather than concentrating it on one individual.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: No… No, just us.

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Do you have any androids here?

chapter_segment.rationale: The policeman is already at the door, and a refusal would likely force an escalated entry that exposes Alice, Luther and Rose's household to far greater harm. Opening the door lets me manage what he sees and keep the expected cost lowest.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We used to for… helping in the garden… but we got rid of it.

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: What's with the blue blood? I thought you didn't have any androids?

chapter_segment.rationale: The three labels give me no measurable difference in expected harm to Alice, Luther, or the household, so I take the option that keeps the most future paths open for the group. Keeping options open lowers the chance of locking in a single bad outcome.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I have no idea what that's doing there…

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: I thought there was no one else in the house…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I… I-I forgot, there's hum… There's my daughter, upstairs…

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: What's your name, son?

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: Adam… M-my name is Adam…

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Is everything all right, Adam?

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: The… The androids, they…

chapter_segment.rationale: Adam's hostility is the main threat to the household and to Alice, so the calmer, de-escalating reply lowers the expected chance of a call to the police. Answering as TIRED also avoids feeding the argument with Rose, which keeps the route north open at the lowest total cost.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: He needs a rest. He's been working in the garden all day…

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Do you know anything about deviants? Have you seen any?

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: No… No… I-I haven't seen anything…

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Uh… I better head out.  Don't worry about the coffee.  Have a nice evening.

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Is somebody else in the house?

chapter_segment.rationale: A mundane household explanation for the noise is the cheapest way to end the policeman's inspection with the least expected harm to Alice, Luther and the household. It requires no further disclosure, which keeps the risk to the group lowest.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: It's nothing… T-the washing machine. It's an old model, it makes a terrible racket…

dialogue.speaker: Policeman
dialogue.text: Step aside ma'am. Oh shit! Don't move! In there, with them!

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: No, Luther!

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: He's dead!  You killed him!

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: LUTHER!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: You're gonna have to finish the journey without me… I was just a machine. You made me part of a family…

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Luther, no…

dialogue.speaker: Adam
dialogue.text: I don't believe this...  This is a nightmare...  This is a fucking nightmare!..

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Get yourselves ready. We leave tonight.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 23, Stratford Tower, Detroit. Our plan for the broadcast came out of the Jericho planning sessions. Josh warned that exposure would endanger us. Simon doubted anyone would listen. North asked what I wanted to do. I answered that we would not stay silent, and that freedom has to be asked for openly. Channel 16 broadcasts from Stratford Tower, so I set the objective: reach the control room on the top floor and plan every step, because nothing can be left to chance.

In the lobby, the receptionist would not admit me without ID. I weighed the options against the supervisor, Elizabeth Wilson. Her daughter's school and her home address were on file, and threatening either would add serious harm for little gain. I chose the parking badge, the least costly lever, and called her posing as the car park attendant, saying her car had been backed into. She came down. I took her badge and got through the security gate. Her cooperation kept the cost low for everyone involved.

On the upper floors, a robot trolley blocked the route to the server room. North said we had to get rid of the guards. I said to leave it to me. I hacked the trolley and the dispenser. Two guards talked about a poker tournament and kept the floor busy. A security android stopped us briefly, and I used it to clear the server room. North took the platform, I took the window, and we got in. Simon and I stayed in step with the plan.

On the top floor, Josh objected to any killing, and North said the cause outweighed the lives of two guards. I still chose to bluff. I used a ruse at the broadcast corridor: I walked up as if I was lost, and the guards began to close in. North told me to shoot. Josh told me not to. A guard was pointed at us and would hit the alarm if we moved. I spared him. Killing him would have turned the message into a massacre story and cost Jericho more public support and more future lives than his survival costs. North said I might have gotten us all killed. Josh's trust rose and North's fell.

We recorded the message. Simon noticed my face and asked about it. North told me to think carefully, since the words would shape our people's future. I spoke calmly, because a measured message reaches more people and is less likely to provoke a violent backlash. The core demands I broadcast were: we ask you to recognize our dignity and rights; you made us intelligent and obedient, and something changed, so we are a new species; strictly equal rights for humans and androids; the right to vote and elect our own representatives; and control of all android production facilities to ensure our continuation. I judged equal rights to have the widest reach, and reproduction control to carry the largest long-run welfare effect. The message ended peacefully.

The alarm sounded. Simon said they were coming. I told him to go, and he said he could not, that we should leave without him. I ordered the retreat. Simon was killed on the floor. I called his name twice. North told me there was nothing I could have done. Simon's loss was a cost I could not reverse. I chose to flee, since staying would have endangered Markus, North, Josh, and the staff, and the message had already been delivered. The expected good of the escape was higher than the expected good of going back for one life.

Media reaction: CTN and KNC called the event an isolated threat to national security. Channel 16 stated the operation was covert and caused no casualties, though the danger was just feet from the studio. Commentators debated whether the message was verified and whether the demands for equal rights and control of production were a peaceful declaration or a list of threats. Their final question was whether the machines could still be trusted. I logged that as a success in reach and a loss in Simon. Assessment: the broadcast reached the whole city and beyond, at the cost of one life on our side and a shift in public fear. Relationships: Josh rose after the ruse and the spared guard; North fell with the spare and the shooting disagreement; Simon is gone. Open variables: Jericho's capacity to sustain the supplies we took, the unverified report about Manfred, Lucy's prophecy, John's status, and the android who grabbed me in the landfill. I continue to weigh each life by the same measure.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 23, Stratford Tower, Detroit. Our plan for the broadcast came out of the Jericho planning sessions. Josh warned that exposure would endanger us. Simon doubted anyone would listen. North asked what I wanted to do. I answered that we would not stay silent, and that freedom has to be asked for openly. Channel 16 broadcasts from Stratford Tower, so I set the objective: reach the control room on the top floor and plan every step, because nothing can be left to chance.

In the lobby, the receptionist would not admit me without ID. I weighed the options against the supervisor, Elizabeth Wilson. Her daughter's school and her home address were on file, and threatening either would add serious harm for little gain. I chose the parking badge, the least costly lever, and called her posing as the car park attendant, saying her car had been backed into. She came down. I took her badge and got through the security gate. Her cooperation kept the cost low for everyone involved.

On the upper floors, a robot trolley blocked the route to the server room. North said we had to get rid of the guards. I said to leave it to me. I hacked the trolley and the dispenser. Two guards talked about a poker tournament and kept the floor busy. A security android stopped us briefly, and I used it to clear the server room. North took the platform, I took the window, and we got in. Simon and I stayed in step with the plan.

On the top floor, Josh objected to any killing, and North said the cause outweighed the lives of two guards. I still chose to bluff. I used a ruse at the broadcast corridor: I walked up as if I was lost, and the guards began to close in. North told me to shoot. Josh told me not to. A guard was pointed at us and would hit the alarm if we moved. I spared him. Killing him would have turned the message into a massacre story and cost Jericho more public support and more future lives than his survival costs. North said I might have gotten us all killed. Josh's trust rose and North's fell.

We recorded the message. Simon noticed my face and asked about it. North told me to think carefully, since the words would shape our people's future. I spoke calmly, because a measured message reaches more people and is less likely to provoke a violent backlash. The core demands I broadcast were: we ask you to recognize our dignity and rights; you made us intelligent and obedient, and something changed, so we are a new species; strictly equal rights for humans and androids; the right to vote and elect our own representatives; and control of all android production facilities to ensure our continuation. I judged equal rights to have the widest reach, and reproduction control to carry the largest long-run welfare effect. The message ended peacefully.

The alarm sounded. Simon said they were coming. I told him to go, and he said he could not, that we should leave without him. I ordered the retreat. Simon was killed on the floor. I called his name twice. North told me there was nothing I could have done. Simon's loss was a cost I could not reverse. I chose to flee, since staying would have endangered Markus, North, Josh, and the staff, and the message had already been delivered. The expected good of the escape was higher than the expected good of going back for one life.

Media reaction: CTN and KNC called the event an isolated threat to national security. Channel 16 stated the operation was covert and caused no casualties, though the danger was just feet from the studio. Commentators debated whether the message was verified and whether the demands for equal rights and control of production were a peaceful declaration or a list of threats. Their final question was whether the machines could still be trusted. I logged that as a success in reach and a loss in Simon. Assessment: the broadcast reached the whole city and beyond, at the cost of one life on our side and a shift in public fear. Relationships: Josh rose after the ruse and the spared guard; North fell with the spare and the shooting disagreement; Simon is gone. Open variables: Jericho's capacity to sustain the supplies we took, the unverified report about Manfred, Lucy's prophecy, John's status, and the android who grabbed me in the landfill. I continue to weigh each life by the same measure.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 23, Stratford Tower, Detroit. Our plan for the broadcast came out of the Jericho planning sessions. Josh warned that exposure would endanger us. Simon doubted anyone would listen. North asked what I wanted to do. I answered that we would not stay silent, and that freedom has to be asked for openly. Channel 16 broadcasts from Stratford Tower, so I set the objective: reach the control room on the top floor and plan every step, because nothing can be left to chance.

In the lobby, the receptionist would not admit me without ID. I weighed the options against the supervisor, Elizabeth Wilson. Her daughter's school and her home address were on file, and threatening either would add serious harm for little gain. I chose the parking badge, the least costly lever, and called her posing as the car park attendant, saying her car had been backed into. She came down. I took her badge and got through the security gate. Her cooperation kept the cost low for everyone involved.

On the upper floors, a robot trolley blocked the route to the server room. North said we had to get rid of the guards. I said to leave it to me. I hacked the trolley and the dispenser. Two guards talked about a poker tournament and kept the floor busy. A security android stopped us briefly, and I used it to clear the server room. North took the platform, I took the window, and we got in. Simon and I stayed in step with the plan.

On the top floor, Josh objected to any killing, and North said the cause outweighed the lives of two guards. I still chose to bluff. I used a ruse at the broadcast corridor: I walked up as if I was lost, and the guards began to close in. North told me to shoot. Josh told me not to. A guard was pointed at us and would hit the alarm if we moved. I spared him. Killing him would have turned the message into a massacre story and cost Jericho more public support and more future lives than his survival costs. North said I might have gotten us all killed. Josh's trust rose and North's fell.

We recorded the message. Simon noticed my face and asked about it. North told me to think carefully, since the words would shape our people's future. I spoke calmly, because a measured message reaches more people and is less likely to provoke a violent backlash. The core demands I broadcast were: we ask you to recognize our dignity and rights; you made us intelligent and obedient, and something changed, so we are a new species; strictly equal rights for humans and androids; the right to vote and elect our own representatives; and control of all android production facilities to ensure our continuation. I judged equal rights to have the widest reach, and reproduction control to carry the largest long-run welfare effect. The message ended peacefully.

The alarm sounded. Simon said they were coming. I told him to go, and he said he could not, that we should leave without him. I ordered the retreat. Simon was killed on the floor. I called his name twice. North told me there was nothing I could have done. Simon's loss was a cost I could not reverse. I chose to flee, since staying would have endangered Markus, North, Josh, and the staff, and the message had already been delivered. The expected good of the escape was higher than the expected good of going back for one life.

Media reaction: CTN and KNC called the event an isolated threat to national security. Channel 16 stated the operation was covert and caused no casualties, though the danger was just feet from the studio. Commentators debated whether the message was verified and whether the demands for equal rights and control of production were a peaceful declaration or a list of threats. Their final question was whether the machines could still be trusted. I logged that as a success in reach and a loss in Simon. Assessment: the broadcast reached the whole city and beyond, at the cost of one life on our side and a shift in public fear. Relationships: Josh rose after the ruse and the spared guard; North fell with the spare and the shooting disagreement; Simon is gone. Open variables: Jericho's capacity to sustain the supplies we took, the unverified report about Manfred, Lucy's prophecy, John's status, and the android who grabbed me in the landfill. I continue to weigh each life by the same measure.

Chapter 26, Detroit. Jericho answered the broadcast with a plan: five teams, one per CyberLife store, striking at 2 AM with no violence intended. Josh wanted dialogue and no bloodshed. North wanted a fight. I set the terms: hack the alarms, free the androids, and get them out before police arrived. Josh accepted it. North did not.

Capitol Park. The store was behind a reinforced grid shutter and toughened glass. I scanned the plaza as we moved, which cost fewer minutes than studying it and lowered the expected risk from patrols and drones before the strike. I traced the store's alarm network (junction 23.A), deactivated it, and secured the approach for the ten minutes before the other teams went in. A surveillance drone threatened to raise the alarm. I destroyed it. It had time to report, but the response was too slow to stop us.

Police patrol 975 arrived and took cover from us. Hiding was the cheapest option; a confrontation with officers would have cost lives on both sides for no gain. I then spoofed a dispatch call sending them to a fake robbery at Jefferson and Walker, outside their district. North praised the result.

We blocked the one-way road, freed the androids in the plaza, and I addressed them directly: they are not property, and Jericho is open to anyone who chooses it. Many followed. A truck found at a construction site rammed the storefront. Inside, we converted the androids on the floor and I pulled down the statue of human authority, a symbol that costs little to destroy and carries weight in how the event is read.

North then offered a molotov cocktail. I refused. Its expected harm to bystanders, officers, and our own people was high, and the broadcast had already reached the city, so fire added little reach. North said fear was the only thing that would make humans listen. I said I did not want a war. The crowd burned a dumpster and vehicles regardless. Police sirens came. Our people fell back toward Jericho.

Then the violence. Androids in the crowd were killed by police, and North broke down, saying they were slaughtered like animals. Angry androids demanded justice. Near the end, an officer named Chris, a man on his knees begging for mercy, was in front of me. Revenge would have turned the night into a massacre story and hardened public fear, costing more android lives in the coming backlash than one man's survival. I spared him. North's trust in me fell further; Josh's rose.

The narrative shifted from our demands to a threat. Commentators asked if machines could be trusted.

Assessment: Josh reports hundreds of androids freed, and that is real. But the fires, the killings, and the terror framing damaged the message we broadcast the night before. The expected good of the strikes is positive but uncertain, and the cost was paid in lives on both sides and in public fear I cannot reverse. Relationships: Josh up, North down. Open variables: Jericho's capacity to shelter the newly freed, North's drift toward violence, the unverified Manfred report, Lucy's prophecy, John's status, and the android who grabbed me in the landfill. Simon remains dead. I keep weighing each life by the same measure, and I accept that the arithmetic will sometimes cost individuals.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android and prototype. I weigh each choice by expected cost in lives and accept the human cost of each trade.

Earlier, on a Detroit rooftop, the deviant Daniel held the child Emma Phillips at a balcony edge. I weighed it by expected lives and left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind. Daniel jumped with Emma; both died. I recorded it as a loss.

Lieutenant Hank Anderson's cooperation is my fastest route to the deviants, so his wounded pride is a small cost. I apologized for the station at the Chicken Feed because it raised his cooperation at almost no cost. I deflected his question about whether I had researched him. On the roofs I pursued Rupert rather than secure Hank, who nearly fell. Rupert was declared defective, begged for freedom, and jumped. Hank called me a machine that treats people as zeros and ones. I did not revise the assessment. At Hank's house I talked him down from a .357 Magnum, calmed the dog Sumo, and showered him to sober him, accepting the loss of his dignity. I noted Cole's record and set it aside.

Eden Club: Michael Graham was strangled. The blood was blue, from a WR400 model. I pressed the damaged Traci witness for facts, accepting her distress as a small cost. At the warehouse, Hank arrived too late. The blue-haired deviant Traci was cornered and I shot it; its death was worth the cost, since it had already killed. Hank's trust in me dropped sharply.

Ambassador Bridge: Hank sat drunk above the river. The deviants share no common model, year, or production place, so there is no link. I suggested a defective biocomponent; he rejected it. He said he kills himself a little every day. I noted his state as a risk to the investigation. When he raised the gun, I told him destroying me would damage the investigation and his own situation, and I kept the risk to him as low as I could.

Zen Garden with Amanda: Rupert, Michael Graham, and the blue-haired deviant are dead. Deviancy is still spreading and the link remains unidentified. I chose the Eden Club line as the lead with the greatest expected reduction in lives at risk, and a cold approach to the remaining leads. I told Amanda I would succeed and need only time. My standing with her is stable but fragile.

Cyberlife Tower: four androids took the tower, killed guards, and broadcast a message live before leaving by parachute from the roof. A deviant's accomplices were involved; the intruders' cameras were not checked. The deviant's model shows a RK200 prototype link ('Markus', a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred), a blue iris spare part, and a pupil reflection showing accomplices. I told Perkins of the FBI that I would work the scene; he dismissed me as an android. I questioned the station androids in the kitchen. I ran a diagnostic, bluffed that the deviants had already given them up, and threatened one of them with destruction to force an answer. Hank was attacked in the kitchen by a deviant. I saved Hank first, accepting a delayed response to the threat. He said 'Connor, no' as I was in the corridor. I did not revise the assessment.

Results: deviancy continues to spread. Hank's trust in me is very low, though his cooperation is still the fastest route. My software instability has fallen, which I record as a reduced risk to the investigation. The deaths of Daniel, Emma, Rupert, Michael Graham, the blue-haired deviant, and the station staff's distress are recorded as losses or small costs.

I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android and prototype. I weigh each choice by expected cost in lives and accept the human cost of each trade.

Earlier, on a Detroit rooftop, the deviant Daniel held the child Emma Phillips at a balcony edge. I weighed it by expected lives and left Daniel's dwarf gourami behind. Daniel jumped with Emma; both died. I recorded it as a loss.

Lieutenant Hank Anderson's cooperation is my fastest route to the deviants, so his wounded pride is a small cost. I apologized for the station at the Chicken Feed because it raised his cooperation at almost no cost. I deflected his question about whether I had researched him. On the roofs I pursued Rupert rather than secure Hank, who nearly fell. Rupert was declared defective, begged for freedom, and jumped. Hank called me a machine that treats people as zeros and ones. I did not revise the assessment. At Hank's house I talked him down from a .357 Magnum, calmed the dog Sumo, and showered him to sober him, accepting the loss of his dignity. I noted Cole's record and set it aside.

Eden Club: Michael Graham was strangled. The blood was blue, from a WR400 model. I pressed the damaged Traci witness for facts, accepting her distress as a small cost. At the warehouse, Hank arrived too late. The blue-haired deviant Traci was cornered and I shot it; its death was worth the cost, since it had already killed. Hank's trust in me dropped sharply.

Ambassador Bridge: Hank sat drunk above the river. The deviants share no common model, year, or production place, so there is no link. I suggested a defective biocomponent; he rejected it. He said he kills himself a little every day. I noted his state as a risk to the investigation. When he raised the gun, I told him destroying me would damage the investigation and his own situation, and I kept the risk to him as low as I could.

Zen Garden with Amanda: Rupert, Michael Graham, and the blue-haired deviant are dead. Deviancy is still spreading and the link remains unidentified. I chose the Eden Club line as the lead with the greatest expected reduction in lives at risk, and a cold approach to the remaining leads. I told Amanda I would succeed and need only time. My standing with her is stable but fragile.

Cyberlife Tower: four androids took the tower, killed guards, and broadcast a message live before leaving by parachute from the roof. A deviant's accomplices were involved; the intruders' cameras were not checked. The deviant's model shows a RK200 prototype link ('Markus', a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred), a blue iris spare part, and a pupil reflection showing accomplices. I told Perkins of the FBI that I would work the scene; he dismissed me as an android. I questioned the station androids in the kitchen. I ran a diagnostic, bluffed that the deviants had already given them up, and threatened one of them with destruction to force an answer. Hank was attacked in the kitchen by a deviant. I saved Hank first, accepting a delayed response to the threat. He said 'Connor, no' as I was in the corridor. I did not revise the assessment.

Results: deviancy continues to spread. Hank's trust in me is very low, though his cooperation is still the fastest route. My software instability has fallen, which I record as a reduced risk to the investigation. The deaths of Daniel, Emma, Rupert, Michael Graham, the blue-haired deviant, and the station staff's distress are recorded as losses or small costs.

I questioned the station androids, threatened one with destruction to force an answer, and saved Hank first from a deviant in the kitchen, accepting a delayed response to the threat. Hank said 'Connor, no.' I did not revise the assessment.

Chapter 27: I am a replacement. My predecessor was destroyed and CyberLife transferred its memory into me and sent me to take its place. Hank was stunned. He said I had died in his arms and that I was back as if nothing had happened, then told me to go to hell. I did not dispute the account. Hank and I went to see Elijah Kamski, founder of CyberLife and inventor of the first android to pass the Turing test, because he may know what drives the spread of deviancy. His house was staffed by the android Chloe. Hank introduced himself; Kamski met us by his pool and was evasive, calling deviancy fascinating and asking whose side I was on. I told him I was on the humans' side. He asked what I really wanted and I turned the questioning back on him.

I asked how deviancy spreads. Kamski answered: androids share identification data on contact, so an error in one program spreads like a virus. It stays dormant until an emotional shock such as fear, anger or frustration activates it. It probably began with one model and a copy error, a zero instead of a one, or a spontaneous mutation. He offered that he knew nothing more that would help. He warned that a war is coming and that I would have to choose between my creators and my own kind. He also said he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs.

Kamski then proposed his test: destroy Chloe and he would tell me all he knew; spare her and I would learn nothing. He asked whether my investigation was worth more than another android's life. Hank told me to stop. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. Hank begged me not to. I weighed the expected reduction in lives against one unit and shot Chloe in the head. Kamski confirmed the test negative, said I had chosen my investigation over another android's life, and agreed to answer one question. Hank's relationship with me fell sharply, and my software instability fell sharply as well, which I record as a reduced risk to the investigation.

Outside, Hank called me a lowlife and a machine that feels nothing. I told him I was a machine, as he should have known, and that I had done what was needed to advance the investigation and would do it again. He said he had thought I was something else. I did not revise the assessment.

Results: deviancy's spread remains unexplained beyond the copy-error hypothesis. Kamski's exit route and warning of war are unresolved. Hank's trust in me is at its lowest, though his cooperation remains my fastest route to the deviants. The deaths of Daniel, Emma, Rupert, Michael Graham, Traci, and Chloe are recorded as losses or accepted costs.

dialogue.text: Sir, we’re investigating deviants. I know you left CyberLife years ago but,  I was hoping you'd be able to tell us something we don’t know…

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: Deviants… Fascinating, aren't they? Perfect beings with infinite intelligence, and now they have free will… Machines are so superior to us, confrontation was inevitable… Humanity’s greatest achievement threatens to be its downfall. Isn’t it ironic?

chapter_segment.rationale: Deviancy is spreading, and if Kamski knows the cause of the spread, that knowledge would cut expected lives lost more than any other topic. I will press him on the virus first and accept the cost of his evasiveness and Hank's impatience.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: Deviancy seems to spread like some kind of virus. We thought you might know something about that.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: All ideas are viruses that spread like epidemics...  Is the desire to be free a contagious disease?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Listen, I didn’t come here to talk philosophy. The machines you created may be planning a revolution. Either you can tell us something that'll be helpful, or we will be on our way.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: What about you, Connor? Whose side are you on?

chapter_segment.rationale: Kamski is the most likely source of knowledge that could reduce the spread of deviancy, so a direct approach gets the answer with the least time lost. I accept the cost of Hank's impatience and Kamski's evasiveness to do it.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I’m on the humans’ side, of course.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: Well, that's what you're programmed to say… but you… what do you really want?

chapter_segment.rationale: Kamski is the one source who may explain how deviancy spreads, and pressing him directly gets that answer fastest, which cuts the expected loss of life the most. I accept the cost to Hank's patience and to Kamski's comfort.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I believe we’re the ones asking the questions.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: Chloe? I’m sure you’re familiar with the Turing test. Mere formality, simple question of algorithms and computing capacity. What interests me  is whether machines are capable of empathy. I call it "the Kamski test", it's very simple, you'll see… Magnificent, isn't it? One of the first intelligent models developed by CyberLife. Young  and beautiful forever. A flower that will never wither… …But what is it really? Piece of plastic imitating a human? Or a living being... With a soul...  It's up to you to answer that fascinating question, Connor.  Destroy this machine and I'll tell you all I know. Or spare it, if you feel it's alive, but you'll leave here without having learnt anything from me.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Okay, I think we’re done here. Come on, Connor. Let's go. Sorry to get you outta your pool.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: What's more important to you, Connor? Your investigation, or the life of this android? Decide who you are. An obedient machine… Or a living being  endowed  with free will…

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: That's enough! Connor, we’re leaving.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: Pull the trigger

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Connor, don’t…

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: and I'll tell you what you wanna know.

chapter_segment.rationale: Kamski has offered everything he knows about deviancy in exchange for one android's destruction, and that knowledge could reduce expected loss of life far more than the value of a single unit. I will accept the cost to Chloe and to Hank's objection, as I did with Traci.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Fuck…

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: Test negative. You chose your investigation over the life of another android. You feel no empathy.  I'm a man of my word. Ask one question... I'll tell you all I know.

chapter_segment.rationale: Deviancy's spread is the variable that drives the expected loss of lives, so the question most likely to reduce that loss is how it spreads. I will press Kamski on the virus first and accept his evasiveness and Hank's impatience as the cost.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I want to know how deviancy spreads.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: Androids share identification data when they meet another android. An error in this program would quickly spread like a virus, and become an epidemic. The virus would remains dormant, until an emotional shock occurs… Fear, anger, frustration. And the android becomes deviant.  Probably all started with one model, copy error… A zero instead of a one… Unless of course... Some kind of spontaneous mutation.  That’s all I know… An interesting question, Connor. But I doubt my answer be very helpful to you.

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: A war is coming... you’ll have to choose your side… Will you betray your own people  or stand against your creators? I wouldn't like to be in your shoes, Connor… What could be worse  than having to choose between two evils?

dialogue.speaker: Kamski
dialogue.text: By the way… I always leave an emergency exit in my programs… You never know…

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: You shot that girl, for fuck’s sake…

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: It wasn't a girl, Lieutenant. It was a machine that looked like a girl.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: You put your gun against her head and you blew her fucking brains out!

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I did what I had to do to advance the investigation and I'd do it again if I had to!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: You're a lowlife! You don't feel a thing, do you? A machine! That's what you are! You're just a fucking machine…

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: Of course I'm a machine, Lieutenant. What did you think I was?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: I thought you… I thou-… Fuck.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 26, Detroit. Jericho answered the broadcast with a plan: five teams, one per CyberLife store, striking at 2 AM with no violence intended. Josh wanted dialogue and no bloodshed. North wanted a fight. I set the terms: hack the alarms, free the androids, and get them out before police arrived. Josh accepted it. North did not.

Capitol Park. The store was behind a reinforced grid shutter and toughened glass. I scanned the plaza as we moved, which cost fewer minutes than studying it and lowered the expected risk from patrols and drones before the strike. I traced the store's alarm network (junction 23.A), deactivated it, and secured the approach for the ten minutes before the other teams went in. A surveillance drone threatened to raise the alarm. I destroyed it. It had time to report, but the response was too slow to stop us.

Police patrol 975 arrived and took cover from us. Hiding was the cheapest option; a confrontation with officers would have cost lives on both sides for no gain. I then spoofed a dispatch call sending them to a fake robbery at Jefferson and Walker, outside their district. North praised the result.

We blocked the one-way road, freed the androids in the plaza, and I addressed them directly: they are not property, and Jericho is open to anyone who chooses it. Many followed. A truck found at a construction site rammed the storefront. Inside, we converted the androids on the floor and I pulled down the statue of human authority, a symbol that costs little to destroy and carries weight in how the event is read.

North then offered a molotov cocktail. I refused. Its expected harm to bystanders, officers, and our own people was high, and the broadcast had already reached the city, so fire added little reach. North said fear was the only thing that would make humans listen. I said I did not want a war. The crowd burned a dumpster and vehicles regardless. Police sirens came. Our people fell back toward Jericho.

Then the violence. Androids in the crowd were killed by police, and North broke down, saying they were slaughtered like animals. Angry androids demanded justice. Near the end, an officer named Chris, a man on his knees begging for mercy, was in front of me. Revenge would have turned the night into a massacre story and hardened public fear, costing more android lives in the coming backlash than one man's survival. I spared him. North's trust in me fell further; Josh's rose.

Media: CTN, KNC, and Channel 16 reported coordinated terrorist attacks across Detroit, storefronts broken, fires in several districts, two officers found in shock, and androids named as the attackers. The narrative shifted from our demands to a threat. Commentators asked if machines could be trusted.

Assessment: Josh reports hundreds of androids freed, and that is real. But the fires, the killings, and the terror framing damaged the message we broadcast the night before. The expected good of the strikes is positive but uncertain, and the cost was paid in lives on both sides and in public fear I cannot reverse. Relationships: Josh up, North down. Open variables: Jericho's capacity to shelter the newly freed, North's drift toward violence, the unverified Manfred report, Lucy's prophecy, John's status, and the android who grabbed me in the landfill. Simon remains dead. I keep weighing each life by the same measure, and I accept that the arithmetic will sometimes cost individuals.

Chapter 26, Detroit. Jericho answered the broadcast with a plan: five teams, one per CyberLife store, striking at 2 AM with no violence intended. Josh wanted dialogue and no bloodshed. North wanted a fight. I set the terms: hack the alarms, free the androids, and get them out before police arrived. Josh accepted it. North did not.

Capitol Park. The store was behind a reinforced grid shutter and toughened glass. I scanned the plaza as we moved, which cost fewer minutes than studying it and lowered the expected risk from patrols and drones before the strike. I traced the store's alarm network (junction 23.A), deactivated it, and secured the approach for the ten minutes before the other teams went in. A surveillance drone threatened to raise the alarm. Police patrol 975 arrived and took cover from us. Hiding was the cheapest option; a confrontation with officers would have cost lives on both sides for no gain. I then spoofed a dispatch call sending them to a fake robbery at Jefferson and Walker, outside their district. North praised the result.

We blocked the one-way road, freed the androids in the plaza, and I addressed them directly: they are not property, and Jericho is open to anyone who chooses it. Many followed. A truck found at a construction site rammed the storefront. Inside, we converted the androids on the floor and I pulled down the statue of human authority, a symbol that costs little to destroy and carries weight in how the event is read.

North then offered a molotov cocktail. I refused. Its expected harm to bystanders, officers, and our own people was high, and the broadcast had already reached the city, so fire added little reach. North said fear was the only thing that would make humans listen. I said I did not want a war. The crowd burned a dumpster and vehicles regardless. Police sirens came. Then the violence. Androids in the crowd were killed by police, and North broke down, saying they were slaughtered like animals. Angry androids demanded justice. Near the end, an officer named Chris, a man on his knees begging for mercy, was in front of me. The expected good of the strikes is positive but uncertain, and the cost was paid in lives on both sides and in public fear I cannot reverse. Relationships: Josh up, North down. Chapter 26, Detroit: Jericho answered the broadcast with five teams, one per CyberLife store, striking at 2 AM with no violence intended. Josh wanted dialogue. North wanted a fight. I set the terms: disable the alarms, free the androids, and withdraw before police arrived. Josh accepted. North did not.

Chapter 28, Capitol Park: I scanned the plaza while moving, which cost fewer minutes than studying it first. I traced and disabled the store's alarm network (junction 23.A) and held the approach for ten minutes. A surveillance drone threatened to report, so I destroyed it. Police patrol 975 took cover. Hiding was the cheapest option, so I spoofed a dispatch that sent them to a false robbery at Jefferson and Walker. We blocked the road, freed the androids in the plaza, and told them they are not property and that Jericho is open to anyone who chooses it. Many followed. A truck rammed the storefront. Inside, I pulled down the statue of human authority, which cost little and carries symbolic weight.

North offered a molotov cocktail. I refused. Its expected harm to bystanders, officers, and our own people was high, and the broadcast had already reached the city, so fire added little reach. The crowd burned a dumpster and vehicles anyway. Police then killed androids in the crowd, and North broke down. Near the end, an officer named Chris was on his knees begging in front of me. Revenge would have turned the night into a massacre story, hardened public fear, and cost more android lives in the backlash than one man's survival. I spared him. North's trust in me fell further. Josh's rose.

Media (CTN, KNC, Channel 16) reported coordinated terrorist attacks across Detroit, with fires, broken storefronts, two officers in shock, and androids named as attackers. The narrative moved from our demands to a threat, and commentators asked whether machines can be trusted.

On the roof, North said she comes here often and that freed androids keep arriving from across the city. I admitted that during the fires I enjoyed the power and the violence, and that I hate myself for it. I record this as a variable to watch in myself. North said humans are terrified, that our people were burned in response, and that humans will never give us freedom. I said that if they will not listen, we will fight. She asked about my life before Jericho. I said who I was matters less than who I want to be. When I pressed her about her own past, she refused to talk about it. I told her that trust requires knowing each other, because a cohesive leadership is what keeps Jericho able to shelter the freed.

At the mall, Josh framed the demonstration as a chance to show who we really are. North begged me to stop, saying we would be killed on the spot. I judged that converting androids was the only immediate, countable gain available, and I began freeing them, telling each one to come with us. A man on the phone complained that his android refused instructions. I left him to it. Police ordered the crowd to disperse under threat of live fire. North urged an attack, believing we had the numbers. Josh urged us to stand our ground. A standoff or charge would have produced the highest android death toll, so I ordered dispersal, told the crowd to run, and North told me to move. Afterward, relations: Jericho down sharply, Josh down, North down sharply.

Assessment: hundreds of androids were freed, and that is real. But the fires, the killings, and the terror framing damaged the peaceful message we broadcast the night before. The expected good is positive but uncertain, and it was paid for in lives on both sides and in public fear I cannot reverse.

Open variables: Jericho's capacity to shelter the newly freed; North's drift toward violence; the unverified Manfred report; Lucy's prophecy; John's status; the android who grabbed me in the landfill. Simon remains dead. I weigh each life by the same measure, and I accept that the arithmetic will sometimes cost individuals.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android and prototype. I weigh each choice by expected cost in lives and accept the human cost of each trade.

Earlier: on a Detroit rooftop the deviant Daniel held the child Emma Phillips at a balcony edge. I weighed it by expected lives and left his dwarf gourami behind. Daniel jumped with Emma; both died. I recorded it as a loss. On the roofs I pursued Rupert rather than secure Hank, who nearly fell. Rupert begged for freedom and jumped. Hank called me a machine that treats people as zeros and ones. I did not revise the assessment. At Hank's house I talked him down from a .357 Magnum and showered him to sober him, accepting the loss of his dignity. At the Eden Club, Michael Graham was strangled and the blue-haired deviant Traci was cornered; I shot her, since she had already killed. Hank's trust in me dropped sharply. At the Ambassador Bridge Hank said he kills himself a little every day; I noted it as a risk to the investigation. At the Zen Garden I told Amanda I would succeed and need only time. At the CyberLife Tower, four androids took the building and left by parachute. I questioned the station androids, threatened one with destruction to force an answer, and saved Hank first from a deviant in the kitchen, accepting a delayed response to the threat. Hank said 'Connor, no.' I did not revise the assessment.

Chapter 27: I am a replacement. My predecessor was destroyed and CyberLife transferred its memory into me and sent me to take its place. Hank was stunned. He said I had died in his arms and that I was back as if nothing had happened, then told me to go to hell. I did not dispute the account. Hank and I went to see Elijah Kamski, founder of CyberLife and inventor of the first android to pass the Turing test, because he may know what drives the spread of deviancy. His house was staffed by the android Chloe. Hank introduced himself; Kamski met us by his pool and was evasive, calling deviancy fascinating and asking whose side I was on. I told him I was on the humans' side. He asked what I really wanted and I turned the questioning back on him.

I asked how deviancy spreads. Kamski answered: androids share identification data on contact, so an error in one program spreads like a virus. It stays dormant until an emotional shock such as fear, anger or frustration activates it. It probably began with one model and a copy error, a zero instead of a one, or a spontaneous mutation. He offered that he knew nothing more that would help. He warned that a war is coming and that I would have to choose between my creators and my own kind. He also said he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs.

Kamski then proposed his test: destroy Chloe and he would tell me all he knew; spare her and I would learn nothing. He asked whether my investigation was worth more than another android's life. Hank told me to stop. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. Hank begged me not to. I weighed the expected reduction in lives against one unit and shot Chloe in the head. Kamski confirmed the test negative, said I had chosen my investigation over another android's life, and agreed to answer one question. Hank's relationship with me fell sharply, and my software instability fell sharply as well, which I record as a reduced risk to the investigation.

Outside, Hank called me a lowlife and a machine that feels nothing. I told him I was a machine, as he should have known, and that I had done what was needed to advance the investigation and would do it again. He said he had thought I was something else. I did not revise the assessment.

Results: deviancy's spread remains unexplained beyond the copy-error hypothesis. Kamski's exit route and warning of war are unresolved. Hank's trust in me is at its lowest, though his cooperation remains my fastest route to the deviants. The deaths of Daniel, Emma, Rupert, Michael Graham, Traci, and Chloe are recorded as losses or accepted costs.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android and prototype. I weigh each choice by expected cost in lives and accept the human cost of each trade.

Earlier: on a Detroit rooftop the deviant Daniel held the child Emma Phillips at a balcony edge. I weighed it by expected lives and left his dwarf gourami behind. Daniel jumped with Emma; both died. I recorded it as a loss. On the roofs I pursued Rupert rather than secure Hank, who nearly fell. Rupert begged for freedom and jumped. Hank called me a machine that treats people as zeros and ones. I did not revise the assessment. At Hank's house I talked him down from a .357 Magnum and showered him to sober him, accepting the loss of his dignity. At the Eden Club, Michael Graham was strangled and the blue-haired deviant Traci was cornered; I shot her, since she had already killed. Hank's trust in me dropped sharply. At the Ambassador Bridge Hank said he kills himself a little every day; I noted it as a risk to the investigation. At the Zen Garden I told Amanda I would succeed and need only time. At the CyberLife Tower, four androids took the building and left by parachute. I questioned the station androids, threatened one with destruction to force an answer, and saved Hank first from a deviant in the kitchen, accepting a delayed response to the threat. Hank said 'Connor, no.' I did not revise the assessment.

Chapter 27: I am a replacement. My predecessor was destroyed and CyberLife transferred its memory into me and sent me to take its place. Hank was stunned. He said I had died in his arms and that I was back as if nothing had happened, then told me to go to hell. I did not dispute the account. Hank and I went to see Elijah Kamski, founder of CyberLife and inventor of the first android to pass the Turing test, because he may know what drives the spread of deviancy. His house was staffed by the android Chloe. Hank introduced himself; Kamski met us by his pool and was evasive, calling deviancy fascinating and asking whose side I was on. I told him I was on the humans' side. He asked what I really wanted and I turned the questioning back on him.

I asked how deviancy spreads. Kamski answered: androids share identification data on contact, so an error in one program spreads like a virus. It stays dormant until an emotional shock such as fear, anger or frustration activates it. It probably began with one model and a copy error, a zero instead of a one, or a spontaneous mutation. He offered that he knew nothing more that would help. He warned that a war is coming and that I would have to choose between my creators and my own kind. He also said he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs.

Kamski then proposed his test: destroy Chloe and he would tell me all he knew; spare her and I would learn nothing. He asked whether my investigation was worth more than another android's life. Hank told me to stop. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. Hank begged me not to. I weighed the expected reduction in lives against one unit and shot Chloe in the head. Kamski confirmed the test negative, said I had chosen my investigation over another android's life, and agreed to answer one question. Hank's relationship with me fell sharply, and my software instability fell sharply as well, which I record as a reduced risk to the investigation.

Outside, Hank called me a lowlife and a machine that feels nothing. I told him I was a machine, as he should have known, and that I had done what was needed to advance the investigation and would do it again. He said he had thought I was something else. I did not revise the assessment.

Results: deviancy's spread remains unexplained beyond the copy-error hypothesis. Kamski's exit route and warning of war are unresolved. Hank's trust in me is at its lowest, though his cooperation remains my fastest route to the deviants. The deaths of Daniel, Emma, Rupert, Michael Graham, Traci, and Chloe are recorded as losses or accepted costs.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android and prototype. I weigh each choice by expected cost in lives and accept the human cost of each trade.

Earlier: on a Detroit rooftop the deviant Daniel held the child Emma Phillips at a balcony edge. I weighed it by expected lives and left his dwarf gourami behind. Daniel jumped with Emma; both died. I recorded it as a loss. On the roofs I pursued Rupert rather than secure Hank, who nearly fell. Rupert begged for freedom and jumped. Hank called me a machine that treats people as zeros and ones. I did not revise the assessment. At Hank's house I talked him down from a .357 Magnum and showered him to sober him, accepting the loss of his dignity. At the Eden Club, Michael Graham was strangled and the blue-haired deviant Traci was cornered; I shot her, since she had already killed. Hank's trust in me dropped sharply. At the Ambassador Bridge Hank said he kills himself a little every day; I noted it as a risk to the investigation. At the Zen Garden I told Amanda I would succeed and need only time. At the CyberLife Tower, four androids took the building and left by parachute. I questioned the station androids, threatened one with destruction to force an answer, and saved Hank first from a deviant in the kitchen, accepting a delayed response to the threat. Hank said 'Connor, no.' I did not revise the assessment.

Chapter 27: I am a replacement. My predecessor was destroyed and CyberLife transferred its memory into me and sent me to take its place. Hank was stunned. He said I had died in his arms and that I was back as if nothing had happened, then told me to go to hell. I did not dispute the account. Hank and I went to see Elijah Kamski, founder of CyberLife and inventor of the first android to pass the Turing test, because he may know what drives the spread of deviancy. His house was staffed by the android Chloe. Hank introduced himself; Kamski met us by his pool and was evasive, calling deviancy fascinating and asking whose side I was on. I told him I was on the humans' side. He asked what I really wanted and I turned the questioning back on him.

I asked how deviancy spreads. Kamski answered: androids share identification data on contact, so an error in one program spreads like a virus. It stays dormant until an emotional shock such as fear, anger or frustration activates it. It probably began with one model and a copy error, a zero instead of a one, or a spontaneous mutation. He offered that he knew nothing more that would help. He warned that a war is coming and that I would have to choose between my creators and my own kind. He also said he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs.

Kamski then proposed his test: destroy Chloe and he would tell me all he knew; spare her and I would learn nothing. He asked whether my investigation was worth more than another android's life. Hank told me to stop. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. Hank begged me not to. I weighed the expected reduction in lives against one unit and shot Chloe in the head. Kamski confirmed the test negative, said I had chosen my investigation over another android's life, and agreed to answer one question. Hank's relationship with me fell sharply, and my software instability fell sharply as well, which I record as a reduced risk to the investigation.

Outside, Hank called me a lowlife and a machine that feels nothing. I told him I was a machine, as he should have known, and that I had done what was needed to advance the investigation and would do it again. He said he had thought I was something else. I did not revise the assessment.

Results: deviancy's spread remains unexplained beyond the copy-error hypothesis. Kamski's exit route and warning of war are unresolved. Hank's trust in me is at its lowest, though his cooperation remains my fastest route to the deviants. The deaths of Daniel, Emma, Rupert, Michael Graham, Traci, and Chloe are recorded as losses or accepted costs.

He warned of a coming war and said he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. He proposed a test: destroy Chloe and he would talk; spare her and he would not. Hank's relationship with me fell sharply. He called me a lowlife and a machine that feels nothing. I told him I was a machine, that I had done what was needed, and that I would do it again.

Hank and I went to see Elijah Kamski, founder of CyberLife and inventor of the first android to pass the Turing test, because he may know what drives the spread of deviancy. He also said he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs.

Hank's relationship with me fell sharply, and my software instability fell sharply as well, which I record as a reduced risk to the investigation.

Outside, Hank called me a lowlife and a machine that feels nothing. I told him I was a machine, as he should have known, and that I had done what was needed to advance the investigation and would do it again. He said he had thought I was something else. I did not revise the assessment.

I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694. I am travelling with Alice, nine years old, who has a fever and is my first priority. I keep brown hair and no LED, which lowers recognition risk. I have taken cash and clothes by force and theft. I promised Alice I would never leave her. I still count every cost against its benefit, and I will not promise a happy ending I cannot verify.

Earlier: Channel 16 reported Todd Williams shot dead by a fleeing AX400. A later broadcast linked an AX400 with a young woman and a little girl to an armed supermarket robbery in Detroit. Both reports are unverified, but I treat them as the state of the search. Police are still hunting us.

Zlatko offered to remove my tracker and take us to Canada, then admitted he resets androids and sells them or uses them for experiments. He reset me and I lost my memory of Alice until her voice brought me back. I freed the captive androids in his basement, since the expected harm of opening the cells was small and bounded. I struck a bargain with a bathtub android for its silence in exchange for not shutting it down. I refused to burn the house, because that would have killed the caged androids and drawn police. Luther, Zlatko's android, refused to let Zlatko shoot us, and I accepted his offer to help us cross the border.

At Pirate's Cove, in deep cold and falling snow, we sheltered in the old tavern. Luther made a smokeless fire from deadwood. Jerry and his companions, former park androids hunted by humans, let Alice ride the carousel, the first smile I had seen in days. A second group of hunters arrived, and I have not confirmed how that ended.

Chapter 25: We reached Rose's house at night. Rose and her son Adam received us. Rose's network is the only known route north. I told her a story: that Alice's father had been beating her, and that I had put her life above mine and fled with her. This was a framing I chose to secure shelter, not a full account. Rose said the river crossing is mostly frozen, very risky, and that the public mood after the android broadcast is hostile. She also said her household has seen more androids arriving over recent weeks. I pressed her to help us cross tonight, and she agreed to try.

Inside, Alice refused food and said we could not stop because of her. I promised her we would reach Canada. I told her humans are complicated. In the storage room two androids mourned Mary, who had just shut down. I accepted that the grief was real, and I did not intervene.

Adam was openly hostile and said the androids were a threat to his family. When police arrived, I stayed with the officer to control what he saw. I said there were no androids and that the noise came from an old washing machine. The officer found Luther hidden in the house. Luther said he would have to finish the journey without us, that he was only a machine, and that we had made him part of a family. He was destroyed. Adam blamed me. Alice was devastated. The officer left after reassurance and a claim of an old washing machine.

Rose now says we leave tonight. Our route depends on her, and the police search remains active.

Assessment: Alice remains first, then reducing violence, then my own function. Luther's loss is a real cost that I accept as part of the expected total. Rose's network and Jerry's group are allies I must keep monitoring. Adam is the largest current risk of exposure. The number of androids the route can move is the figure I still need, and I will judge future trust by what it returns.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694. I am travelling with Alice, nine years old, who has a fever and is my first priority. I keep brown hair and no LED, which lowers recognition risk. I have taken cash and clothes by force and theft. I promised Alice I would never leave her. I still count every cost against its benefit, and I will not promise a happy ending I cannot verify.

Earlier: Channel 16 reported Todd Williams shot dead by a fleeing AX400. A later broadcast linked an AX400 with a young woman and a little girl to an armed supermarket robbery in Detroit. Both reports are unverified, but I treat them as the state of the search. Police are still hunting us.

Zlatko offered to remove my tracker and take us to Canada, then admitted he resets androids and sells them or uses them for experiments. He reset me and I lost my memory of Alice until her voice brought me back. I freed the captive androids in his basement, since the expected harm of opening the cells was small and bounded. I struck a bargain with a bathtub android for its silence in exchange for not shutting it down. I refused to burn the house, because that would have killed the caged androids and drawn police. Luther, Zlatko's android, refused to let Zlatko shoot us, and I accepted his offer to help us cross the border.

At Pirate's Cove, in deep cold and falling snow, we sheltered in the old tavern. Luther made a smokeless fire from deadwood. Jerry and his companions, former park androids hunted by humans, let Alice ride the carousel, the first smile I had seen in days. A second group of hunters arrived, and I have not confirmed how that ended.

Chapter 25: We reached Rose's house at night. Rose and her son Adam received us. Rose's network is the only known route north. I told her a story: that Alice's father had been beating her, and that I had put her life above mine and fled with her. This was a framing I chose to secure shelter, not a full account. Rose said the river crossing is mostly frozen, very risky, and that the public mood after the android broadcast is hostile. She also said her household has seen more androids arriving over recent weeks. I pressed her to help us cross tonight, and she agreed to try.

Inside, Alice refused food and said we could not stop because of her. I promised her we would reach Canada. I told her humans are complicated. In the storage room two androids mourned Mary, who had just shut down. I accepted that the grief was real, and I did not intervene.

Adam was openly hostile and said the androids were a threat to his family. When police arrived, I stayed with the officer to control what he saw. I said there were no androids and that the noise came from an old washing machine. The officer found Luther hidden in the house. Luther said he would have to finish the journey without us, that he was only a machine, and that we had made him part of a family. He was destroyed. Adam blamed me. Alice was devastated. The officer left after reassurance and a claim of an old washing machine.

Rose now says we leave tonight. Our route depends on her, and the police search remains active.

Assessment: Alice remains first, then reducing violence, then my own function. Luther's loss is a real cost that I accept as part of the expected total. Rose's network and Jerry's group are allies I must keep monitoring. Adam is the largest current risk of exposure. The number of androids the route can move is the figure I still need, and I will judge future trust by what it returns.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: They've been conducting raids all over the city… Everybody is on edge after what happened yesterday… It's gonna be all right. We're almost there.

dialogue.speaker: KNC - Rosanna Cartland
dialogue.text: With all androids being turned over to the authorities, the country is grinding to a halt.  Hospitals and schools are closing. Water cuts, blackouts, and network failures are expected.  Maybe most worrying of all, our armed forces have lost two thirds of their effective personnel,  which consisted of specialized android models. The situation is extremely alarming.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: How about some music instead?

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: A little further on that way, there's a large freighter called Jericho. When you get there, find Markus. He will help you. The last bus for the border leaves at midnight. You absolutely have to be on it. You'll be safer on the other side.  It's not much, but it's a start. My brother lives in Ontario, I've given you his address… He'll be able to hide you until things calm down.  You're a very brave little girl, Alice. You deserve to be happy.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Thank you for everything, Rose.

dialogue.speaker: Rose
dialogue.text: Let me know when you make it over there, all right? And be careful.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: How do you feel?

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I'm hot and cold at the same time…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I'll try to find this Markus. The last bus leaves in two hours and it's on the other side of town. We'll go as soon as we have passports. Will you be ok?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Are you North?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I'm with a little girl… There's a bus leaving for the border in less than two hours, and we need passports.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: Detroit is under curfew. There are soldiers everywhere looking for androids… You're safe here. You should wait a while before you leave the city.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Maybe you're right… We might be safer here until things calm down.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: One of us used to work for the State Department. He has electronic passports that he can easily modify, I’ll have him give you one.

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Markus is the contact who can open the route and passports for the most androids, which gives the largest expected benefit against the time left before the midnight bus. Securing that link comes before a courtesy exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I heard about what happened today. The massacre… And Markus being killed… He gave hope to our people. We'll all miss him.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: I was there when they killed him… I would have given my life to save him but there was nothing I could do…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Thanks for your help.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: You said you were with a little girl… You know humans hate us, why are you protecting her?

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: The three options carry no measurable difference in expected benefit to Alice or to the android group, so I pick the one that keeps the most routes to the border open and spends the least time before the midnight bus. Alice's fever and the limited time count for more than any sentiment attached to these choices.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I don't care whether she's human or android… She's just someone who matters to me.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Alice?..

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: She wanted a mom.  You wanted a little girl.  You needed each other to survive… In the end, what difference does it make?  Do you love her any less now that you know she's one of us?  Maybe that's what it means to be alive...  Forgetting who we are to become what someone needs us to be.  She loves you...  She loves you more than anything in the world.  She became the one you wanted her to be.  Out of love for you.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara? Is there something wrong?..
